# sval 2.20.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/sval/2.20.0

## What is it?

`sval` is a serialization-only framework for Rust. It has a simple, but capable design that can express any Rust data structure, plus some it can't yet. It was originally designed as a niche framework for structured logging, targeting serialization to [JSON](https://www.json.org), [protobuf](https://protobuf.dev), and Rust's [Debug-style formatting](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/trait.Debug.html). The project has evolved beyond this point into a fully general framework for introspecting runtime data.

The core of `sval` is the [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) trait. It defines the data model and features of the framework.

`sval` has made a few different API design decisions compared to [to better accommodate the needs of Rust diagnostic frameworks:](https://serde.rs)

`serde`- **Simple API.**The- `Stream`
- `dyn`-friendly.- `Stream`- `dyn`-compatible without intermediate boxing, making it possible to use in no-std environments.
- **Buffer-friendly.**The- `Stream`
- **Borrowing as an optimization.**The- `Stream`- `'sval`, but is also required to accept temporary ones too. This makes it possible to optimize away allocations where possible, but still force them if it's required.
- **Broadly compatible.**- `sval`imposes very few constraints of its own, so it can trivially translate implementations of- `serde::Serialize`- `sval::Value`

`sval`'s data model takes inspiration from [CBOR](https://cbor.io), specifically:

- **Small core.**The base data model of- `sval`is small. The required members of the- `Stream`
- **Extensible tags.**Users can define- *tags*that extend- `sval`'s data model with new semantics. Examples of tags include Rust's- `Some`and- `None`variants, constant-sized arrays, text that doesn't require JSON escaping, and anything else you might need.

## Getting started

This section is a high-level guided tour of `sval`'s design and API. To get started, add `sval` to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "2.20.0"
 = ["derive"]
```
### Serializing values

As a quick example, here's how you can use `sval` to serialize a runtime value as JSON.

First, add [ sval_json](https://docs.rs/sval_json/2.20.0/sval_json/index.html) to your

`Cargo.toml`:```
[]
 = "2.20.0"
 = ["std"]
```
Next, derive the [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Value.html) trait on the type you want to serialize, including on any other types it uses in its fields:

```
```
Finally, use [ stream_to_string](https://docs.rs/sval_json/2.20.0/sval_json/fn.stream_to_string.html) to serialize an instance of your type as JSON:

```
let my_record = MyRecord ;
// Produces:
//
// {"field_0":1,"field_1":true,"field_2":"some text"}
let json: String = stream_to_string?;
```
### The `Value` trait

The previous example didn't reveal a lot of detail about how `sval` works, only that there's a [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Value.html) trait involved, and it somehow allows us to convert an instance of the

`MyRecord` struct into a JSON object. Using [, we can peek behind the covers and see what the](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-expand)

`cargo expand``Value` trait does. The previous example expands to something like this:```
```
The [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Value.html) trait has a single required method,

`stream`, which is responsible for driving an instance of a [with its fields. The](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`[trait defines](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``sval`'s data model and the mechanics of how data is described in it. In this example, the `MyRecord` struct is represented as a *record tuple*, a type that can be either a

*record*with fields named by a

[, or a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Label.html)

`Label`*tuple*with fields indexed by an

[. Labels and indexes can be annotated with a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Index.html)

`Index`[which add user-defined semantics to them. In this case, the labels carry the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[tag meaning they're valid Rust identifiers, and the indexes carry the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/tags/constant.VALUE_IDENT.html)

`VALUE_IDENT`[tag meanings they're zero-indexed field offsets. The specific type of](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/tags/constant.VALUE_OFFSET.html)

`VALUE_OFFSET`[can decide whether to treat the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``MyRecord` type as either a record (in the case of JSON) or a tuple (in the case of protobuf), and whether it understands that tags it sees or not.### The `Stream` trait

Something to notice about the [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) API in the expanded

`MyRecord` example is that it is *flat*. The call to

`record_tuple_begin` doesn't return a new type like `serde`'s `serialize_struct` does. The implementor of [is responsible for issuing the correct sequence of](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Value.html)

`Value`[calls as it works through its structure. The](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`[can then rely on markers like](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``record_tuple_value_begin` and `record_tuple_value_end` to know what position within a value it is without needing to track that state itself. The flat API makes dyn-compatibility and buffering simpler, but makes implementing non-trivial streams more difficult, because you can't rely on recursion to manage state.Recall the way `MyRecord` was converted into JSON earlier:

```
let json: String = stream_to_string?;
```
Internally, [ stream_to_string](https://docs.rs/sval_json/2.20.0/sval_json/fn.stream_to_string.html) uses an instance of

[that writes JSON tokens for each piece of the value it encounters. For example,](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``record_tuple_begin` and `record_tuple_end` will emit the corresponding `{` `}` characters for a JSON object.`sval`'s data model is *layered*. The required methods on [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) represent the base data model that more expressive constructs map down to. Here's what a minimal

[that just formats values in](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``sval`'s base data model looks like:```
;
let my_record = MyRecord ;
// Prints:
//
// [["field_0",1,],["field_1",true,],["field_2","some text",],],
stream;
```
Recall that the `MyRecord` struct mapped to a `record_tuple` in `sval`'s data model. `record_tuple`s in turn are represented in the base data model as a sequence of 2-dimensional sequences where the first element is the field label and the second is its value.

[ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)s aren't limited to just serializing data into interchange formats. They can manipulate or interrogate a value any way it likes. Here's an example of a

[that attempts to extract a specific field of a value as an](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``i32`:```
let my_record = MyRecord ;
assert_eq!;
```
### Streaming text

Strings in `sval` don't need to be streamed in a single call. As an example, say we have a template type like this:

```
;
```
If we wanted to serialize `Template` to a string, we could implement [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Value.html), handling each literal and property as a separate fragment:

```
```
When streamed as JSON, `Template` would produce something like this:

```
let template = Template;
// Produces:
//
// "some literal text and {x} and more literal text"
let json = stream_to_string?;
```
### Borrowed data

The [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) trait carries a

`'sval` lifetime it can use to accept borrowed text and binary values. Borrowing in `sval` is an optimization. Even if a [uses a concrete](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``'sval` lifetime, it still needs to handle computed values. Here's an example of a [that attempts to extract a borrowed string from a value by making use of the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``'sval` lifetime:```
```
Implementations of [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Value.html) should provide a

[with borrowed data where possible, and only compute it if it needs to.](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`### Error handling

`sval`'s [ Error](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Error.html) type doesn't carry any state of its own. It only signals early termination of the

[which may be because its job is done, or because it failed. It's up to the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`[to carry whatever state it needs to provide meaningful errors.](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`## Data model

This section descibes `sval`'s data model in detail using examples in Rust syntax. Some types in `sval`'s model aren't representable in Rust yet, so they use pseudo syntax.

### Base model

#### Nulls

```
null
```
```
stream.null?;
```
#### Booleans

```
bool
```
```
stream.bool?;
```
#### 64bit signed integers

```
i64
```
```
stream.i64?;
```
#### Text

```
```
```
stream.text_begin?;
stream.text_fragment?;
stream.text_fragment?;
stream.text_end?;
```
Note that `sval` text is an array of strings.

#### Sequences

```
```
```
stream.seq_begin?;
stream.seq_value_begin?;
stream.i64?;
stream.seq_value_end?;
stream.seq_value_begin?;
stream.bool?;
stream.seq_value_end?;
stream.seq_end?;
```
Note that Rust arrays are homogeneous, but `sval` sequences are heterogeneous.

### Extended model

#### 8bit unsigned integers

```
u8
```
```
stream.u8?;
```
8bit unsigned integers reduce to 64bit signed integers in the base model.

#### 16bit unsigned integers

```
u16
```
```
stream.u16?;
```
16bit unsigned integers reduce to 64bit signed integers in the base model.

#### 32bit unsigned integers

```
u32
```
```
stream.u32?;
```
32bit unsigned integers reduce to 64bit signed integers in the base model.

#### 64bit unsigned integers

```
u64
```
```
stream.u64?;
```
64bit unsigned integers reduce to 64bit signed integers in the base data model if they fit, or base10 ASCII text if they don't.

#### 128bit unsigned integers

```
u128
```
```
stream.u128?;
```
128bit unsigned integers reduce to 64bit signed integers in the base data model if they fit, or base10 ASCII text if they don't.

#### 8bit signed integers

```
i8

```
8bit signed integers reduce to 64bit signed integers in the base model.

#### 16bit signed integers

```
16bit signed integers reduce to 64bit signed integers in the base model.

#### 32bit signed integers

32bit signed integers reduce to 64bit signed integers in the base model.

#### 128bit signed integers

```
i128
```

stream.i128?;

128bit signed integers reduce to 64bit signed integers in the base data model if they fit, or base10 ASCII text if they don't.

#### 32bit binary floating point numbers

#### Binary

#### Maps

#### Tags

#### User-defined tags

`sval` tags, tagged values, records, tuples, enums, and their values can carry a user-defined [ Tag](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Tag.html) that alters their semantics. A

[may understand a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`[and treat its annotated value differently, or it may ignore them. An example of a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[is](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[, which is for text that encodes an arbitrary-precision decimal floating point number with a standardized format. A](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/tags/constant.NUMBER.html)

`NUMBER`[may parse these numbers and encode them differently to regular text.](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`Here's an example of a user-defined [ Tag](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Tag.html) for treating integers as Unix timestamps, and a

[that understands them:](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream````
// Define a tag as a constant.
//
// Tags are expected to have unique names.
//
// The rules of our tag are that 64bit unsigned integers that carry it are seconds since
// the Unix epoch.
pub const UNIX_TIMESTAMP: Tag = new;
// Derive `Value` on a type, annotating it with our tag.
//
// We could also implement `Value` manually using `stream.tagged_begin(Some(&UNIX_TIMESTAMP), ..)`.
;
// Here's an example of a `Stream` that understands our tag.
```
The [ Label](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Label.html) and

[types can also carry a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Index.html)

`Index`[. An example of a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[you might use on a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[is](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Label.html)

`Label`[, for labels that hold a valid Rust identifier.](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/tags/constant.VALUE_IDENT.html)

`VALUE_IDENT`### Type system

`sval` has an implicit structural type system based on the sequence of calls a [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) receives, and the values of any

[,](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Label.html)

`Label`[, or](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Index.html)

`Index`[on them, with the following exceptions:](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`- Text type does not depend on the composition of fragments, or on their length.
- Binary type does not depend on the composition of fragments, or on their length.
- Sequences are untyped. Their type doesn't depend on the types of their elements, or on their length.
- Maps are untyped. Their type doesn't depend on the types of their keys or values, or on their length.
- Enums holding differently typed variants have the same type.

These rules may be better formalized in the future.

## Ecosystem

`sval` is a general framework with specific serialization formats and utilities provided as external libraries:

- `sval_fmt`
- `sval_json`- `serde`-compatible format.
- `sval_protobuf`
- `sval_serde`- `serde`and- `sval`.
- `sval_buffer`- `Value`
- `sval_flatten`- `#[serde(flatten)]`.
- `sval_nested`- `sval`'s flat- `Stream`- `serde`'s. For types that- `#[derive(Value)]`, the translation is non-allocating.
- `sval_ref`- `Value`- `MyType<'a>`) instead of externally (like- `&'a MyType`).

                    sval 2.20.0

# sval - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/sval/2.20.0/target-redirect/sval/

## Expand description

Structured, streaming values.

`sval` is a serialization framework that treats data as a flat stream of tokens.
The source of that data could be some Rust object or parsed from some encoding.
It’s well suited to self-describing, text-based formats like JSON.

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting started

For a complete introduction, see [the project readme](https://github.com/sval-rs/sval).

Add `sval` to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies.sval]
version = "2.20.0"
```
By default, `sval` doesn’t depend on Rust’s standard library or integrate with its collection types.
To include them, add the `alloc` or `std` Cargo features:

```
[dependencies.sval]
version = "2.20.0"
features = ["std"]
```
`sval` provides procedural macros for deriving its traits.
Add the `derive` Cargo feature to enable them:

```
[dependencies.sval]
version = "2.20.0"
features = ["derive"]
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-value-trait)The `Value` trait

[ Value](https://docs.rs/trait.Value.html) is a trait for data types to implement that surfaces their structure through visitors called

*streams*.

`Value` is like `serde`’s `Serialize`. It can also be used like `serde`’s `Deserialize`.Many standard types in Rust implement the `Value` trait. It can be derived on your own types using the `sval_derive` library.

[§](https://docs.rs#the-stream-trait)The `Stream` trait

[ Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.Stream.html) is a trait for data formats and visitors to implement that observes the structure of

*values*.

`Stream` is like `serde`’s `Serializer`. It can also be used like `serde`’s `Deserializer`.[§](https://docs.rs#data-model)Data-model

`sval`’s data-model is defined by the [ Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.Stream.html) trait. It includes:

- Null
- Booleans (`true`,`false`)
- Text blobs
- Binary blobs
- Integers (`u8`-`u128`,`i8`-`i128`)
- Binary floating points (`f32`-`f64`)
- Sequences
- Maps
- Tags
- Tagged values
- Records
- Tuples
- Enums

[§](https://docs.rs#tags)Tags

[ Tag](https://docs.rs/struct.Tag.html) is a type for extending

`sval`’s data-model with new kinds of values.
Rust’s own `()` and `Option<T>` types are expressed as tags.
Other examples of tags include text that encodes RFC3339 timestamps or RFC4122 UUIDs.The [ tags](https://docs.rs/tags/index.html) module contains built-in tags.
Other libraries may define their own tags too.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [default_](https://docs.rs/default_stream/index.html)- stream
- Default method implementations for `Stream`
- [default_](https://docs.rs/default_value/index.html)- value
- Default method implementations for `Value`
- [tags](https://docs.rs/tags/index.html)
- Built-in tags for fundamental types.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Binary](https://docs.rs/struct.BinaryArray.html)- Array
- An adapter that streams a slice of 8bit unsigned integers as binary with a fixed size.
- [Binary](https://docs.rs/struct.BinarySlice.html)- Slice
- An adapter that streams a slice of 8bit unsigned integers as binary.
- [Display](https://docs.rs/struct.Display.html)
- Adapt a `fmt::Display``sval::Value`].
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- An error encountered while streaming a value.
- [Index](https://docs.rs/struct.Index.html)
- The index of a value in its parent context.
- [Label](https://docs.rs/struct.Label.html)
- A textual label for some value.
- [MapSlice](https://docs.rs/struct.MapSlice.html)
- An adapter that streams a slice of key-value pairs as a map.
- [Null](https://docs.rs/struct.Null.html)
- The absence of any meaningful value.
- [Tag](https://docs.rs/struct.Tag.html)
- A type tag for a value.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [error](https://docs.rs/fn.error.html)
- A streaming result with a generic failure.
- [stream](https://docs.rs/fn.stream.html)
- Stream a value through a stream.
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_computed.html)- computed
- Stream a value through a stream with an arbitrarily short lifetime.
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_display.html)- display
- Stream a `fmt::Display``Stream`
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_display_fragments.html)- display_ - fragments
- Stream a `fmt::Display``Stream``Stream::text_begin``Stream::text_end`
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_number.html)- number
- Stream an arbitrary precision number conforming to `tags::NUMBER``fmt::Display`

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- A generic streaming result.

[ Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.Stream.html) is a trait for data formats and visitors to implement that observes the structure of

*values*.

`Stream` is like `serde`’s `Serializer`. It can also be used like `serde`’s `Deserializer`.[§](https://docs.rs#data-model)Data-model

`sval`’s data-model is defined by the [ Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.Stream.html) trait. It includes:

- Null
- Booleans (`true`,`false`)
- Text blobs
- Binary blobs
- Integers (`u8`-`u128`,`i8`-`i128`)
- Binary floating points (`f32`-`f64`)
- Sequences
- Maps
- Tags
- Tagged values
- Records
- Tuples
- Enums

[§](https://docs.rs#tags)Tags

[ Tag](https://docs.rs/struct.Tag.html) is a type for extending

`sval`’s data-model with new kinds of values.
Rust’s own `()` and `Option<T>` types are expressed as tags.
Other examples of tags include text that encodes RFC3339 timestamps or RFC4122 UUIDs.The [ tags](https://docs.rs/tags/index.html) module contains built-in tags.
Other libraries may define their own tags too.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [default_](https://docs.rs/default_stream/index.html)- stream
- Default method implementations for `Stream`
- [default_](https://docs.rs/default_value/index.html)- value
- Default method implementations for `Value`
- [tags](https://docs.rs/tags/index.html)
- Built-in tags for fundamental types.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Binary](https://docs.rs/struct.BinaryArray.html)- Array
- An adapter that streams a slice of 8bit unsigned integers as binary with a fixed size.
- [Binary](https://docs.rs/struct.BinarySlice.html)- Slice
- An adapter that streams a slice of 8bit unsigned integers as binary.
- [Display](https://docs.rs/struct.Display.html)
- Adapt a `fmt::Display``sval::Value`].
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- An error encountered while streaming a value.
- [Index](https://docs.rs/struct.Index.html)
- The index of a value in its parent context.
- [Label](https://docs.rs/struct.Label.html)
- A textual label for some value.
- [MapSlice](https://docs.rs/struct.MapSlice.html)
- An adapter that streams a slice of key-value pairs as a map.
- [Null](https://docs.rs/struct.Null.html)
- The absence of any meaningful value.
- [Tag](https://docs.rs/struct.Tag.html)
- A type tag for a value.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [error](https://docs.rs/fn.error.html)
- A streaming result with a generic failure.
- [stream](https://docs.rs/fn.stream.html)
- Stream a value through a stream.
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_computed.html)- computed
- Stream a value through a stream with an arbitrarily short lifetime.
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_display.html)- display
- Stream a `fmt::Display``Stream`
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_display_fragments.html)- display_ - fragments
- Stream a `fmt::Display``Stream``Stream::text_begin``Stream::text_end`
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_number.html)- number
- Stream an arbitrary precision number conforming to `tags::NUMBER``fmt::Display`

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- A generic streaming result.

# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/src/sval/lib.rs.html

# sval/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)/*!
[2](https://docs.rs#2)Structured, streaming values.
[3](https://docs.rs#3)
[4](https://docs.rs#4)`sval` is a serialization framework that treats data as a flat stream of tokens.
[5](https://docs.rs#5)The source of that data could be some Rust object or parsed from some encoding.
[6](https://docs.rs#6)It's well suited to self-describing, text-based formats like JSON.
[7](https://docs.rs#7)
[8](https://docs.rs#8)# Getting started
[9](https://docs.rs#9)
[10](https://docs.rs#10)For a complete introduction, see [the project readme](https://github.com/sval-rs/sval).
[11](https://docs.rs#11)
[12](https://docs.rs#12)Add `sval` to your `Cargo.toml`:
[13](https://docs.rs#13)
[14](https://docs.rs#14)```toml
[15](https://docs.rs#15)[dependencies.sval]
[16](https://docs.rs#16)version = "2.20.0"
[17](https://docs.rs#17)```
[18](https://docs.rs#18)
[19](https://docs.rs#19)By default, `sval` doesn't depend on Rust's standard library or integrate with its collection types.
[20](https://docs.rs#20)To include them, add the `alloc` or `std` Cargo features:
[21](https://docs.rs#21)
[22](https://docs.rs#22)```toml
[23](https://docs.rs#23)[dependencies.sval]
[24](https://docs.rs#24)version = "2.20.0"
[25](https://docs.rs#25)features = ["std"]
[26](https://docs.rs#26)```
[27](https://docs.rs#27)
[28](https://docs.rs#28)`sval` provides procedural macros for deriving its traits.
[29](https://docs.rs#29)Add the `derive` Cargo feature to enable them:
[30](https://docs.rs#30)
[31](https://docs.rs#31)```toml
[32](https://docs.rs#32)[dependencies.sval]
[33](https://docs.rs#33)version = "2.20.0"
[34](https://docs.rs#34)features = ["derive"]
[35](https://docs.rs#35)```
[36](https://docs.rs#36)
[37](https://docs.rs#37)# The `Value` trait
[38](https://docs.rs#38)
[39](https://docs.rs#39)[`Value`] is a trait for data types to implement that surfaces their structure through visitors called _streams_.
[40](https://docs.rs#40)`Value` is like `serde`'s `Serialize`. It can also be used like `serde`'s `Deserialize`.
[41](https://docs.rs#41)
[42](https://docs.rs#42)Many standard types in Rust implement the `Value` trait. It can be derived on your own types using the `sval_derive` library.
[43](https://docs.rs#43)
[44](https://docs.rs#44)# The `Stream` trait
[45](https://docs.rs#45)
[46](https://docs.rs#46)[`Stream`] is a trait for data formats and visitors to implement that observes the structure of _values_.
[47](https://docs.rs#47)`Stream` is like `serde`'s `Serializer`. It can also be used like `serde`'s `Deserializer`.
[48](https://docs.rs#48)
[49](https://docs.rs#49)# Data-model
[50](https://docs.rs#50)
[51](https://docs.rs#51)`sval`'s data-model is defined by the [`Stream`] trait. It includes:
[52](https://docs.rs#52)
[53](https://docs.rs#53)- Null
[54](https://docs.rs#54)- Booleans (`true`, `false`)
[55](https://docs.rs#55)- Text blobs
[56](https://docs.rs#56)- Binary blobs
[57](https://docs.rs#57)- Integers (`u8`-`u128`, `i8`-`i128`)
[58](https://docs.rs#58)- Binary floating points (`f32`-`f64`)
[59](https://docs.rs#59)- Sequences
[60](https://docs.rs#60)- Maps
[61](https://docs.rs#61)- Tags
[62](https://docs.rs#62)- Tagged values
[63](https://docs.rs#63)- Records
[64](https://docs.rs#64)- Tuples
[65](https://docs.rs#65)- Enums
[66](https://docs.rs#66)
[67](https://docs.rs#67)# Tags
[68](https://docs.rs#68)
[69](https://docs.rs#69)[`Tag`] is a type for extending `sval`'s data-model with new kinds of values.
[70](https://docs.rs#70)Rust's own `()` and `Option<T>` types are expressed as tags.
[71](https://docs.rs#71)Other examples of tags include text that encodes RFC3339 timestamps or RFC4122 UUIDs.
[72](https://docs.rs#72)
[73](https://docs.rs#73)The [`tags`] module contains built-in tags.
[74](https://docs.rs#74)Other libraries may define their own tags too.
[75](https://docs.rs#75)*/
[76](https://docs.rs#76)

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

Try convert this value into a 32bit binary floating point number.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

}## Expand description

A consumer of structured data.

Each instance of a stream is expected to receive a single complete value.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Stream null, the absence of any other meaningful value.

Null is a complete value.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/sval/stream.rs.html#46)#### fn [text_begin](https://docs.rs#tymethod.text_begin)(&mut self, num_bytes: [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)>) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/sval/stream.rs.html#46)

#### fn [text_begin](https://docs.rs#tymethod.text_begin)(&mut self, num_bytes: [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)>) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)

Start a UTF8 text string.

After this call, a stream expects a series of zero or more calls to [ Stream::text_fragment](https://docs.rs/trait.Stream.html#method.text_fragment) and

[. A call to](https://docs.rs/trait.Stream.html#tymethod.text_fragment_computed)

`Stream::text_fragment_computed`[completes the value.](https://docs.rs/trait.Stream.html#tymethod.text_end)

`Stream::text_end`This method accepts a `num_bytes` hint, which hints the length of the text value in bytes.
If a value for `num_bytes` is provided, it must be accurate.

Stream a signed 64bit integer.

An integer is a complete value.

Start a heterogeneous sequence of values.

After this call, a stream expects a series of zero or more sequence elements. Each element is a sequence of the following calls:

- `Stream::seq_value_begin`
- A complete value.
- `Stream::seq_value_end`

A call to [ Stream::seq_end](https://docs.rs/trait.Stream.html#tymethod.seq_end) completes the value.

This method accepts a `num_entries` hint, which hints the number of elements in the sequence.
If a value for `num_entries` is provided, it must be accurate.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/sval/stream.rs.html#333)#### fn [seq_value_begin](https://docs.rs#tymethod.seq_value_begin)(&mut self) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/sval/stream.rs.html#333)

#### fn [seq_value_begin](https://docs.rs#tymethod.seq_value_begin)(&mut self) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)

Start an individual value in a sequence.

This method may only be called in the context of a sequence value, after a call to [ Stream::seq_begin](https://docs.rs/trait.Stream.html#tymethod.seq_begin).
This call must be followed by a complete value, then a call to

[. Sequence elements cannot be empty.](https://docs.rs/trait.Stream.html#tymethod.seq_value_end)

`Stream::seq_value_end`[Source](https://docs.rs/src/sval/stream.rs.html#341)#### fn [seq_value_end](https://docs.rs#tymethod.seq_value_end)(&mut self) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/sval/stream.rs.html#341)

#### fn [seq_value_end](https://docs.rs#tymethod.seq_value_end)(&mut self) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)

Complete an individual value in a sequence.

This method may only be called in the context of an element in a sequence value, after a call to [ Stream::seq_value_begin](https://docs.rs/trait.Stream.html#tymethod.seq_value_begin).
Sequence elements cannot be empty.

Start a bitstring.

After this call, a stream expects a series of zero or more calls to [ Stream::binary_fragment](https://docs.rs/trait.Stream.html#method.binary_fragment) and

[. A call to](https://docs.rs/trait.Stream.html#method.binary_fragment_computed)

`Stream::binary_fragment_computed`[completes the value.](https://docs.rs/trait.Stream.html#method.binary_end)

`Stream::binary_end`This method accepts a `num_bytes` hint, which hints the length of the bitstring value in bytes.
If a value for `num_bytes` is provided, it must be accurate.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/sval/stream.rs.html#100-102)#### fn [binary_fragment_computed](https://docs.rs#method.binary_fragment_computed)(&mut self, fragment: &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)

Stream a fragment of a bitstring, borrowed for some arbitrarily short lifetime.

This method may only be called in the context of a bitstring value, between a call to [ Stream::binary_begin](https://docs.rs/trait.Stream.html#method.binary_begin) and

[.](https://docs.rs/trait.Stream.html#method.binary_end)

`Stream::binary_end`Stream an unsigned 8bit integer.

An integer is a complete value.

Stream an unsigned 16bit integer.

An integer is a complete value.

Stream an unsigned 32bit integer.

An integer is a complete value.

Stream an unsigned 64bit integer.

An integer is a complete value.

Stream an unsigned 128bit integer.

An integer is a complete value.

Stream a signed 8bit integer.

An integer is a complete value.

Stream a signed 16bit integer.

An integer is a complete value.

Stream a signed 32bit integer.

An integer is a complete value.

Stream a signed 128bit integer.

An integer is a complete value.

Stream a 32bit binary floating point number.

An integer is a complete value.

Stream a 64bit binary floating point number.

An integer is a complete value.

Start a heterogeneous mapping of arbitrary keys to values.

After this call, a stream expects a series of zero or more map key-value pairs. Each key-value pair is a sequence of the following calls:

- `Stream::map_key_begin`
- A complete value.
- `Stream::map_key_end`
- `Stream::map_value_begin`
- A complete value.
- `Stream::map_value_end`

A call to [ Stream::map_end](https://docs.rs/trait.Stream.html#method.map_end) completes the value.

This method accepts a `num_entries` hint, which hints the number of key-value pairs in the map.
If a value for `num_entries` is provided, it must be accurate.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/sval/stream.rs.html#260-262)#### fn [map_key_begin](https://docs.rs#method.map_key_begin)(&mut self) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/sval/stream.rs.html#260-262)

This call must be followed by a complete value, then a call to

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/sval/stream.rs.html#368-375)

Start a variant in an enumerated type.

After this call, a stream expects a complete value as the enum variant.
An enum variant can be any type that accepts a [ Tag](https://docs.rs/struct.Tag.html),

[, and](https://docs.rs/struct.Label.html)

`Label`[parameter. That includes:](https://docs.rs/struct.Index.html)

`Index`- Tags (`Stream::tag`
- Tagged values (`Stream::tagged_begin`
- Records (`Stream::record_begin`
- Tuples (`Stream::tuple_begin`
- Enums (`Stream::enum_begin`

Enum variants may be empty.

A call to [ Stream::enum_end](https://docs.rs/trait.Stream.html#method.enum_end) completes the value.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/sval/stream.rs.html#429-431)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/sval/stream.rs.html#429-431)

Stream a standalone tag.

Standalone tags are complete values.

Use a tag as a hint without streaming it as a value.

Hints may be given at any point in a stream and may be interpreted by a stream in any way, but can’t be required for a correct result.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/sval/stream.rs.html#458-466)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/sval/stream.rs.html#458-466)

This method accepts a `num_entries` hint, which hints the number of fields in the record.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# Tag in sval - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Tag.html

`pub struct Tag { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A type tag for a value.

Tags are additional hints that a stream may use to interpret a value differently, or to avoid some unnecessary work.

The contents of a tag aren’t considered public, only equality between two tag identifiers.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

# sval::tags - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/tags/index.html

## Expand description

Built-in tags for fundamental types.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [CONSTANT_](https://docs.rs/constant.CONSTANT_SIZE.html)- SIZE
- A tag for values that have a constant size.
- [NUMBER](https://docs.rs/constant.NUMBER.html)
- A tag for arbitrary-precision decimal numbers.
- [RUST_](https://docs.rs/constant.RUST_OPTION_NONE.html)- OPTION_ - NONE
- A tag for a value that represents the `None`variant of a Rust`Option`.
- [RUST_](https://docs.rs/constant.RUST_OPTION_SOME.html)- OPTION_ - SOME
- A tag for a value that represents the `Some`variant of a Rust`Option`.
- [RUST_](https://docs.rs/constant.RUST_UNIT.html)- UNIT
- A tag for Rust’s `()`type.
- [VALUE_](https://docs.rs/constant.VALUE_IDENT.html)- IDENT
- A tag for labels that are valid Rust identifiers.
- [VALUE_](https://docs.rs/constant.VALUE_OFFSET.html)- OFFSET
- A tag for indexes that are zero-based non-negative offsets into a larger structure.

# NUMBER in sval::tags - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/tags/constant.NUMBER.html

A tag for arbitrary-precision decimal numbers.

[§](#valid-datatypes)Valid datatypes

[§](#grammar)Grammar

`^(?<sign>[+-])?(?<integral>[0-9]+)(?:\.(?<fractional>[0-9]+))?(?:[eE](?<expsign>[+-])?(?<exp>[0-9]+))?$`

Examples of valid numbers include:

- `1`
- `+1`
- `-1`
- `001`
- `123.456`
- `1e2`
- `123.456e789`
- `123.456e+789`
- `123.456e-789`

# sval - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sval/latest/sval/

## Expand description

Structured, streaming values.

`sval` is a serialization framework that treats data as a flat stream of tokens.
The source of that data could be some Rust object or parsed from some encoding.
It’s well suited to self-describing, text-based formats like JSON.

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting started

For a complete introduction, see [the project readme](https://github.com/sval-rs/sval).

Add `sval` to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies.sval]
version = "2.20.0"
```
By default, `sval` doesn’t depend on Rust’s standard library or integrate with its collection types.
To include them, add the `alloc` or `std` Cargo features:

```
[dependencies.sval]
version = "2.20.0"
features = ["std"]
```
`sval` provides procedural macros for deriving its traits.
Add the `derive` Cargo feature to enable them:

```
[dependencies.sval]
version = "2.20.0"
features = ["derive"]
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-value-trait)The `Value` trait

[ Value](https://docs.rs/trait.Value.html) is a trait for data types to implement that surfaces their structure through visitors called

*streams*.

`Value` is like `serde`’s `Serialize`. It can also be used like `serde`’s `Deserialize`.Many standard types in Rust implement the `Value` trait. It can be derived on your own types using the `sval_derive` library.

[§](https://docs.rs#the-stream-trait)The `Stream` trait

[ Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.Stream.html) is a trait for data formats and visitors to implement that observes the structure of

*values*.

`Stream` is like `serde`’s `Serializer`. It can also be used like `serde`’s `Deserializer`.[§](https://docs.rs#data-model)Data-model

`sval`’s data-model is defined by the [ Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.Stream.html) trait. It includes:

- Null
- Booleans (`true`,`false`)
- Text blobs
- Binary blobs
- Integers (`u8`-`u128`,`i8`-`i128`)
- Binary floating points (`f32`-`f64`)
- Sequences
- Maps
- Tags
- Tagged values
- Records
- Tuples
- Enums

[§](https://docs.rs#tags)Tags

[ Tag](https://docs.rs/struct.Tag.html) is a type for extending

`sval`’s data-model with new kinds of values.
Rust’s own `()` and `Option<T>` types are expressed as tags.
Other examples of tags include text that encodes RFC3339 timestamps or RFC4122 UUIDs.The [ tags](https://docs.rs/tags/index.html) module contains built-in tags.
Other libraries may define their own tags too.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [default_](https://docs.rs/default_stream/index.html)- stream
- Default method implementations for `Stream`
- [default_](https://docs.rs/default_value/index.html)- value
- Default method implementations for `Value`
- [tags](https://docs.rs/tags/index.html)
- Built-in tags for fundamental types.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Binary](https://docs.rs/struct.BinaryArray.html)- Array

- [Binary](https://docs.rs/struct.BinarySlice.html)- Slice

- [Display](https://docs.rs/struct.Display.html)
- Adapt a `fmt::Display``sval::Value`].

# humantime 2.4.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/humantime/^2

# Human Time

**Status: stable**

[Documentation](https://docs.rs/humantime) |
[Github](https://github.com/tailhook/humantime) |
[Crate](https://crates.io/crates/humantime)

Features:

- Parses durations in free form like `15days 2min 2s`
- Formats durations in similar form `2years 2min 12us`
- Parses and formats timestamp in `rfc3339`format:`2018-01-01T12:53:00Z`
- Parses timestamps in a weaker format: `2018-01-01 12:53:00`

Timestamp parsing/formatting is super-fast because format is basically fixed.

Here are some micro-benchmarks:

```
test result: ok. 0 passed; 0 failed; 26 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out
     Running target/release/deps/datetime_format-8facb4ac832d9770
running 2 tests
test rfc3339_chrono            ... bench:         737 ns/iter (+/- 37)
test rfc3339_humantime_seconds ... bench:          73 ns/iter (+/- 2)
test result: ok. 0 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 2 measured; 0 filtered out
     Running target/release/deps/datetime_parse-342628f877d7867c
running 6 tests
test datetime_utc_parse_millis  ... bench:         228 ns/iter (+/- 11)
test datetime_utc_parse_nanos   ... bench:         236 ns/iter (+/- 10)
test datetime_utc_parse_seconds ... bench:         204 ns/iter (+/- 18)
test rfc3339_humantime_millis   ... bench:          28 ns/iter (+/- 1)
test rfc3339_humantime_nanos    ... bench:          36 ns/iter (+/- 2)
test rfc3339_humantime_seconds  ... bench:          24 ns/iter (+/- 1)
test result: ok. 0 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 6 measured; 0 filtered out
```
See [humantime-serde](https://docs.rs/humantime-serde) for serde integration (previous crate [serde-humantime](https://docs.rs/serde-humantime/0.1.1/serde_humantime/) looks unmaintained).

# sval 2.19.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/sval/2.19.0

## What is it?

`sval` is a serialization-only framework for Rust. It has a simple, but capable design that can express any Rust data structure, plus some it can't yet. It was originally designed as a niche framework for structured logging, targeting serialization to [JSON](https://www.json.org), [protobuf](https://protobuf.dev), and Rust's [Debug-style formatting](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/trait.Debug.html). The project has evolved beyond this point into a fully general framework for introspecting runtime data.

The core of `sval` is the [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) trait. It defines the data model and features of the framework.

`sval` has made a few different API design decisions compared to [to better accommodate the needs of Rust diagnostic frameworks:](https://serde.rs)

`serde`- **Simple API.**The- `Stream`
- `dyn`-friendly.- `Stream`- `dyn`-compatible without intermediate boxing, making it possible to use in no-std environments.
- **Buffer-friendly.**The- `Stream`
- **Borrowing as an optimization.**The- `Stream`- `'sval`, but is also required to accept temporary ones too. This makes it possible to optimize away allocations where possible, but still force them if it's required.
- **Broadly compatible.**- `sval`imposes very few constraints of its own, so it can trivially translate implementations of- `serde::Serialize`- `sval::Value`

`sval`'s data model takes inspiration from [CBOR](https://cbor.io), specifically:

- **Small core.**The base data model of- `sval`is small. The required members of the- `Stream`
- **Extensible tags.**Users can define- *tags*that extend- `sval`'s data model with new semantics. Examples of tags include Rust's- `Some`and- `None`variants, constant-sized arrays, text that doesn't require JSON escaping, and anything else you might need.

## Getting started

This section is a high-level guided tour of `sval`'s design and API. To get started, add `sval` to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "2.19.0"
 = ["derive"]
```
### Serializing values

As a quick example, here's how you can use `sval` to serialize a runtime value as JSON.

First, add [ sval_json](https://docs.rs/sval_json/2.19.0/sval_json/index.html) to your

`Cargo.toml`:```
[]
 = "2.19.0"
 = ["std"]
```
Next, derive the [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/trait.Value.html) trait on the type you want to serialize, including on any other types it uses in its fields:

```
```
Finally, use [ stream_to_string](https://docs.rs/sval_json/2.19.0/sval_json/fn.stream_to_string.html) to serialize an instance of your type as JSON:

```
let my_record = MyRecord ;
// Produces:
//
// {"field_0":1,"field_1":true,"field_2":"some text"}
let json: String = stream_to_string?;
```
### The `Value` trait

The previous example didn't reveal a lot of detail about how `sval` works, only that there's a [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/trait.Value.html) trait involved, and it somehow allows us to convert an instance of the

`MyRecord` struct into a JSON object. Using [, we can peek behind the covers and see what the](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-expand)

`cargo expand``Value` trait does. The previous example expands to something like this:```
```
The [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/trait.Value.html) trait has a single required method,

`stream`, which is responsible for driving an instance of a [with its fields. The](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`[trait defines](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``sval`'s data model and the mechanics of how data is described in it. In this example, the `MyRecord` struct is represented as a *record tuple*, a type that can be either a

*record*with fields named by a

[, or a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/struct.Label.html)

`Label`*tuple*with fields indexed by an

[. Labels and indexes can be annotated with a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/struct.Index.html)

`Index`[which add user-defined semantics to them. In this case, the labels carry the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[tag meaning they're valid Rust identifiers, and the indexes carry the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/tags/constant.VALUE_IDENT.html)

`VALUE_IDENT`[tag meanings they're zero-indexed field offsets. The specific type of](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/tags/constant.VALUE_OFFSET.html)

`VALUE_OFFSET`[can decide whether to treat the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``MyRecord` type as either a record (in the case of JSON) or a tuple (in the case of protobuf), and whether it understands that tags it sees or not.### The `Stream` trait

Something to notice about the [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) API in the expanded

`MyRecord` example is that it is *flat*. The call to

`record_tuple_begin` doesn't return a new type like `serde`'s `serialize_struct` does. The implementor of [is responsible for issuing the correct sequence of](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/trait.Value.html)

`Value`[calls as it works through its structure. The](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`[can then rely on markers like](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``record_tuple_value_begin` and `record_tuple_value_end` to know what position within a value it is without needing to track that state itself. The flat API makes dyn-compatibility and buffering simpler, but makes implementing non-trivial streams more difficult, because you can't rely on recursion to manage state.Recall the way `MyRecord` was converted into JSON earlier:

```
let json: String = stream_to_string?;
```
Internally, [ stream_to_string](https://docs.rs/sval_json/2.19.0/sval_json/fn.stream_to_string.html) uses an instance of

[that writes JSON tokens for each piece of the value it encounters. For example,](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``record_tuple_begin` and `record_tuple_end` will emit the corresponding `{` `}` characters for a JSON object.`sval`'s data model is *layered*. The required methods on [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) represent the base data model that more expressive constructs map down to. Here's what a minimal

[that just formats values in](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``sval`'s base data model looks like:```
;
let my_record = MyRecord ;
// Prints:
//
// [["field_0",1,],["field_1",true,],["field_2","some text",],],
stream;
```
Recall that the `MyRecord` struct mapped to a `record_tuple` in `sval`'s data model. `record_tuple`s in turn are represented in the base data model as a sequence of 2-dimensional sequences where the first element is the field label and the second is its value.

[ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)s aren't limited to just serializing data into interchange formats. They can manipulate or interrogate a value any way it likes. Here's an example of a

[that attempts to extract a specific field of a value as an](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``i32`:```
let my_record = MyRecord ;
assert_eq!;
```
### Streaming text

Strings in `sval` don't need to be streamed in a single call. As an example, say we have a template type like this:

```
;
```
If we wanted to serialize `Template` to a string, we could implement [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/trait.Value.html), handling each literal and property as a separate fragment:

```
```
When streamed as JSON, `Template` would produce something like this:

```
let template = Template;
// Produces:
//
// "some literal text and {x} and more literal text"
let json = stream_to_string?;
```
### Borrowed data

The [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) trait carries a

`'sval` lifetime it can use to accept borrowed text and binary values. Borrowing in `sval` is an optimization. Even if a [uses a concrete](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``'sval` lifetime, it still needs to handle computed values. Here's an example of a [that attempts to extract a borrowed string from a value by making use of the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``'sval` lifetime:```
```
Implementations of [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/trait.Value.html) should provide a

[with borrowed data where possible, and only compute it if it needs to.](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`### Error handling

`sval`'s [ Error](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/struct.Error.html) type doesn't carry any state of its own. It only signals early termination of the

[which may be because its job is done, or because it failed. It's up to the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`[to carry whatever state it needs to provide meaningful errors.](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

#### User-defined tags

`sval` tags, tagged values, records, tuples, enums, and their values can carry a user-defined [ Tag](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/struct.Tag.html) that alters their semantics. A

[may understand a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`[and treat its annotated value differently, or it may ignore them. An example of a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[is](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[, which is for text that encodes an arbitrary-precision decimal floating point number with a standardized format. A](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/tags/constant.NUMBER.html)

`NUMBER`[may parse these numbers and encode them differently to regular text.](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`Here's an example of a user-defined [ Tag](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/struct.Tag.html) for treating integers as Unix timestamps, and a

[that understands them:](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream````
// Define a tag as a constant.
//
// Tags are expected to have unique names.
//
// The rules of our tag are that 64bit unsigned integers that carry it are seconds since
// the Unix epoch.
pub const UNIX_TIMESTAMP: Tag = new;
// Derive `Value` on a type, annotating it with our tag.
//
// We could also implement `Value` manually using `stream.tagged_begin(Some(&UNIX_TIMESTAMP), ..)`.
;
// Here's an example of a `Stream` that understands our tag.
```
The [ Label](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/struct.Label.html) and

[types can also carry a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/struct.Index.html)

`Index`[. An example of a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[you might use on a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[is](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/struct.Label.html)

`Label`[, for labels that hold a valid Rust identifier.](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/tags/constant.VALUE_IDENT.html)

`VALUE_IDENT`### Type system

`sval` has an implicit structural type system based on the sequence of calls a [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) receives, and the values of any

[,](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/struct.Label.html)

`Label`[, or](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/struct.Index.html)

`Index`[on them, with the following exceptions:](https://docs.rs/sval/2.19.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`- Text type does not depend on the composition of fragments, or on their length.
- Binary type does not depend on the composition of fragments, or on their length.
- Sequences are untyped. Their type doesn't depend on the types of their elements, or on their length.
- Maps are untyped. Their type doesn't depend on the types of their keys or values, or on their length.
- Enums holding differently typed variants have the same type.

These rules may be better formalized in the future.

## Ecosystem

`sval` is a general framework with specific serialization formats and utilities provided as external libraries:

- `sval_fmt`
- `sval_json`- `serde`-compatible format.
- `sval_protobuf`
- `sval_serde`- `serde`and- `sval`.
- `sval_buffer`- `Value`
- `sval_flatten`- `#[serde(flatten)]`.
- `sval_nested`- `sval`'s flat- `Stream`- `serde`'s. For types that- `#[derive(Value)]`, the translation is non-allocating.
- `sval_ref`- `Value`- `MyType<'a>`) instead of externally (like- `&'a MyType`).

---

# sval 2.18.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/sval/2.18.0

## What is it?

`sval` is a serialization-only framework for Rust. It has a simple, but expressive design that can express any Rust data structure, plus some it can't yet. It was originally designed as a niche framework for structured logging, targeting serialization to [JSON](https://www.json.org), [protobuf](https://protobuf.dev), and Rust's [Debug-style formatting](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/trait.Debug.html). The project has evolved beyond this point into a fully general and capable framework for introspecting runtime data.

The core of `sval` is the [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) trait. It defines the data model and features of the framework.

`sval` makes a few different API design decisions compared to [, the de-facto choice, to better accommodate the needs of Rust diagnostic frameworks:](https://serde.rs)

`serde`- **Simple API.**The- `Stream`
- `dyn`-friendly.- `Stream`- `dyn`-compatible without intermediate boxing, making it possible to use in no-std environments.
- **Buffer-friendly.**The- `Stream`
- **Borrowing as an optimization.**The- `Stream`- `'sval`, but is also required to accept temporary ones too. This makes it possible to optimize away allocations where possible, but still force them if it's required.
- **Broadly compatible.**- `sval`imposes very few constraints of its own, so it can trivially translate implementations of- `serde::Serialize`- `sval::Value`

`sval`'s data model takes inspiration from [CBOR](https://cbor.io), specifically:

- **Small core.**The base data model of- `sval`is small. The required members of the- `Stream`
- **Extensible tags.**Users can define- *tags*that extend- `sval`'s data model with new semantics. Examples of tags include Rust's- `Some`and- `None`variants, constant-sized arrays, text that doesn't require JSON escaping, and anything else you might need.

## Getting started

This section is a high-level guided tour of `sval`'s design and API. To get started, add `sval` to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "2.18.0"
 = ["derive"]
```
### Serializing values

As a quick example, here's how you can use `sval` to serialize a runtime value as JSON.

```
Next, derive the [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/trait.Value.html) trait on the type you want to serialize, including on any other types it uses in its fields:

```
```
Finally, use [ stream_to_string](https://docs.rs/sval_json/2.18.0/sval_json/fn.stream_to_string.html) to serialize an instance of your type as JSON:

```
let my_record = MyRecord ;
// Produces:
//
// {"field_0":1,"field_1":true,"field_2":"some text"}
let json: String = stream_to_string?;
```
### The `Value` trait

Something to notice about the [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) API in the expanded

`MyRecord` example is that it is *flat*. The call to

`record_tuple_begin` doesn't return a new type like `serde`'s `serialize_struct` does. The implementor of [is responsible for issuing the correct sequence of](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/trait.Value.html)

`Stream``record_tuple_value_begin` and `record_tuple_value_end` to know what position within a value it is without needing to track that state itself. The flat API makes dyn-compatibility and buffering simpler, but makes implementing non-trivial streams more difficult, because you can't rely on recursive to manage state.Recall the way `MyRecord` was converted into JSON earlier:

```

```
Internally, [ stream_to_string](https://docs.rs/sval_json/2.18.0/sval_json/fn.stream_to_string.html) uses an instance of

[that writes JSON tokens for each piece of the value it encounters. For example,](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``record_tuple_begin` and `record_tuple_end` will emit the corresponding `{` `}` characters for a JSON object.`sval`'s data model is *layered*. The required methods on [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) represent the base data model that more expressive constructs map down to. Here's what a minimal

[that just formats values in](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``sval`'s base data model looks like:```
;
let my_record = MyRecord ;
// Prints:
//
// [["field_0",1,],["field_1",true,],["field_2","some text",],],
stream;
```
Recall that the `MyRecord` struct mapped to a `record_tuple` in `sval`'s data model. `record_tuple`s in turn are represented in the base data model as a sequence of 2-dimensional sequences where the first element is the field label and the second is its value.

[ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)s aren't limited to just serializing data into interchange formats. They can manipulate or interrogate a value any way it likes. Here's an example of a

[that attempts to extract a specific field of a value as an](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``i32`:```
let my_record = MyRecord ;
assert_eq!;
```
### Streaming text

Strings in `sval` don't need to be streamed in a single call. As an example, say we have a template type like this:

```
;
```
If we wanted to serialize `Template` to a string, we could implement [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/trait.Value.html), handling each literal and property as a separate fragment:

```
```
When streamed as JSON, `Template` would produce something like this:

```
let template = Template;
// Produces:
//
// "some literal text and {x} and more literal text"
let json = stream_to_string?;
```
### Borrowed data

The [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) trait carries a

`'sval` lifetime it can use to accept borrowed text and binary values. Borrowing in `sval` is an optimization. Even if a [uses a concrete](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``'sval` lifetime, it still needs to handle computed values. Here's an example of a [that attempts to extract a borrowed string from a value by making use of the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``'sval` lifetime:```
```
Implementations of [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/trait.Value.html) should provide a

[with borrowed data where possible, and only compute it if it needs to.](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`### Error handling

`sval`'s [ Error](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/struct.Error.html) type doesn't carry any state of its own. It only signals early termination of the

[which may be because its job is done, or because it failed. It's up to the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`[to carry whatever state it needs to provide meaningful errors.](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

#### User-defined tags

`sval` tags, tagged values, records, tuples, enums, and their values can carry a user-defined [ Tag](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/struct.Tag.html) that alters their semantics. A

[may understand a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`[and treat its annotated value differently, or it may ignore them. An example of a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[is](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[, which is for text that encodes an arbitrary-precision decimal floating point number with a standardized format. A](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/tags/constant.NUMBER.html)

`NUMBER`[may parse these numbers and encode them differently to regular text.](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`Here's an example of a user-defined [ Tag](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/struct.Tag.html) for treating integers as Unix timestamps, and a

[that understands them:](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream````
// Define a tag as a constant.
//
// Tags are expected to have unique names.
//
// The rules of our tag are that 64bit unsigned integers that carry it are seconds since
// the Unix epoch.
pub const UNIX_TIMESTAMP: Tag = new;
// Derive `Value` on a type, annotating it with our tag.
//
// We could also implement `Value` manually using `stream.tagged_begin(Some(&UNIX_TIMESTAMP), ..)`.
;
// Here's an example of a `Stream` that understands our tag.
```
The [ Label](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/struct.Label.html) and

[types can also carry a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/struct.Index.html)

`Index`[. An example of a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[you might use on a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[is](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/struct.Label.html)

`Label`[, for labels that hold a valid Rust identifier.](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/tags/constant.VALUE_IDENT.html)

`VALUE_IDENT`### Type system

`sval` has an implicit structural type system based on the sequence of calls a [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) receives, and the values of any

[,](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/struct.Label.html)

`Label`[, or](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/struct.Index.html)

`Index`[on them, with the following exceptions:](https://docs.rs/sval/2.18.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`- Text type does not depend on the composition of fragments, or on their length.
- Binary type does not depend on the composition of fragments, or on their length.
- Sequences are untyped. Their type doesn't depend on the types of their elements, or on their length.
- Maps are untyped. Their type doesn't depend on the types of their keys or values, or on their length.
- Enums holding differently typed variants have the same type.

These rules may be better formalized in the future.

## Ecosystem

`sval` is a general framework with specific serialization formats and utilities provided as external libraries:

- `sval_fmt`
- `sval_json`- `serde`-compatible format.
- `sval_protobuf`
- `sval_serde`- `serde`and- `sval`.
- `sval_buffer`- `Value`
- `sval_flatten`- `#[serde(flatten)]`.
- `sval_nested`- `sval`'s flat- `Stream`- `serde`'s. For types that- `#[derive(Value)]`, the translation is non-allocating.
- `sval_ref`- `Value`- `MyType<'a>`) instead of externally (like- `&'a MyType`).

---

# sval 2.17.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/sval/2.17.0

## What is it?

`sval` is a serialization-only framework for Rust. It has a simple, but expressive design that can express any Rust data structure, plus some it can't yet. It was originally designed as a niche framework for structured logging, targeting serialization to [JSON](https://www.json.org), [protobuf](https://protobuf.dev), and Rust's [Debug-style formatting](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/trait.Debug.html). The project has evolved beyond this point into a fully general and capable framework for introspecting runtime data.

The core of `sval` is the [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) trait. It defines the data model and features of the framework.

`sval` makes a few different API design decisions compared to [, the de-facto choice, to better accommodate the needs of Rust diagnostic frameworks:](https://serde.rs)

`serde`- **Simple API.**The- `Stream`
- `dyn`-friendly.- `Stream`- `dyn`-compatible without intermediate boxing, making it possible to use in no-std environments.
- **Buffer-friendly.**The- `Stream`
- **Borrowing as an optimization.**The- `Stream`- `'sval`, but is also required to accept temporary ones too. This makes it possible to optimize away allocations where possible, but still force them if it's required.
- **Broadly compatible.**- `sval`imposes very few constraints of its own, so it can trivially translate implementations of- `serde::Serialize`- `sval::Value`

`sval`'s data model takes inspiration from [CBOR](https://cbor.io), specifically:

- **Small core.**The base data model of- `sval`is small. The required members of the- `Stream`
- **Extensible tags.**Users can define- *tags*that extend- `sval`'s data model with new semantics. Examples of tags include Rust's- `Some`and- `None`variants, constant-sized arrays, text that doesn't require JSON escaping, and anything else you might need.

## Getting started

This section is a high-level guided tour of `sval`'s design and API. To get started, add `sval` to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "2.17.0"
 = ["derive"]
```
### Serializing values

As a quick example, here's how you can use `sval` to serialize a runtime value as JSON.

First, add [ sval_json](https://docs.rs/sval_json/2.17.0/sval_json/index.html) to your

`Cargo.toml`:```
[]
 = "2.17.0"
 = ["std"]
```
Next, derive the [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/trait.Value.html) trait on the type you want to serialize, including on any other types it uses in its fields:

```
```
Finally, use [ stream_to_string](https://docs.rs/sval_json/2.17.0/sval_json/fn.stream_to_string.html) to serialize an instance of your type as JSON:

```
let my_record = MyRecord ;
// Produces:
//
// {"field_0":1,"field_1":true,"field_2":"some text"}
let json: String = stream_to_string?;
```
### The `Value` trait

The previous example didn't reveal a lot of detail about how `sval` works, only that there's a [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/trait.Value.html) trait involved, and it somehow allows us to convert an instance of the

`MyRecord` struct into a JSON object. Using [, we can peek behind the covers and see what the](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-expand)

`cargo expand``Value` trait does. The previous example expands to something like this:```
```
The [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/trait.Value.html) trait has a single required method,

`stream`, which is responsible for driving an instance of a [with its fields. The](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`[trait defines](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``sval`'s data model and the mechanics of how data is described in it. In this example, the `MyRecord` struct is represented as a *record tuple*, a type that can be either a

*record*with fields named by a

[, or a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/struct.Label.html)

`Label`*tuple*with fields indexed by an

[. Labels and indexes can be annotated with a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/struct.Index.html)

`Index`[which add user-defined semantics to them. In this case, the labels carry the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[tag meaning they're valid Rust identifiers, and the indexes carry the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/tags/constant.VALUE_IDENT.html)

`VALUE_IDENT`[tag meanings they're zero-indexed field offsets. The specific type of](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/tags/constant.VALUE_OFFSET.html)

`VALUE_OFFSET`[can decide whether to treat the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``MyRecord` type as either a record (in the case of JSON) or a tuple (in the case of protobuf), and whether it understands that tags it sees or not.### The `Stream` trait

Something to notice about the [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) API in the expanded

`MyRecord` example is that it is *flat*. The call to

`record_tuple_begin` doesn't return a new type like `serde`'s `serialize_struct` does. The implementor of [is responsible for issuing the correct sequence of](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/trait.Value.html)

`Value`[calls as it works through its structure. The](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`[can then rely on markers like](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``record_tuple_value_begin` and `record_tuple_value_end` to know what position within a value it is without needing to track that state itself. The flat API makes dyn-compatibility and buffering simpler, but makes implementing non-trivial streams more difficult, because you can't rely on recursive to manage state.Recall the way `MyRecord` was converted into JSON earlier:

```
let json: String = stream_to_string?;
```
Internally, [ stream_to_string](https://docs.rs/sval_json/2.17.0/sval_json/fn.stream_to_string.html) uses an instance of

[that writes JSON tokens for each piece of the value it encounters. For example,](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``record_tuple_begin` and `record_tuple_end` will emit the corresponding `{` `}` characters for a JSON object.`sval`'s data model is *layered*. The required methods on [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) represent the base data model that more expressive constructs map down to. Here's what a minimal

[that just formats values in](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``sval`'s base data model looks like:```
;
let my_record = MyRecord ;
// Prints:
//
// [["field_0",1,],["field_1",true,],["field_2","some text",],],
stream;
```
Recall that the `MyRecord` struct mapped to a `record_tuple` in `sval`'s data model. `record_tuple`s in turn are represented in the base data model as a sequence of 2-dimensional sequences where the first element is the field label and the second is its value.

[ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)s aren't limited to just serializing data into interchange formats. They can manipulate or interrogate a value any way it likes. Here's an example of a

[that attempts to extract a specific field of a value as an](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``i32`:```
let my_record = MyRecord ;
assert_eq!;
```
### Streaming text

Strings in `sval` don't need to be streamed in a single call. As an example, say we have a template type like this:

```
;
```
If we wanted to serialize `Template` to a string, we could implement [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/trait.Value.html), handling each literal and property as a separate fragment:

```
```
When streamed as JSON, `Template` would produce something like this:

```
let template = Template;
// Produces:
//
// "some literal text and {x} and more literal text"
let json = stream_to_string?;
```

`'sval` lifetime it can use to accept borrowed text and binary values. Borrowing in `sval` is an optimization. Even if a [uses a concrete](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``'sval` lifetime, it still needs to handle computed values. Here's an example of a [that attempts to extract a borrowed string from a value by making use of the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``'sval` lifetime:```
```
Implementations of [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/trait.Value.html) should provide a

[with borrowed data where possible, and only compute it if it needs to.](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`### Error handling

`sval`'s [ Error](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/struct.Error.html) type doesn't carry any state of its own. It only signals early termination of the

[which may be because its job is done, or because it failed. It's up to the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`[to carry whatever state it needs to provide meaningful errors.](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)
