#### User-defined tags

`sval` tags, tagged values, records, tuples, enums, and their values can carry a user-defined [ Tag](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/struct.Tag.html) that alters their semantics. A

[may understand a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`[and treat its annotated value differently, or it may ignore them. An example of a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[is](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[, which is for text that encodes an arbitrary-precision decimal floating point number with a standardized format. A](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/tags/constant.NUMBER.html)

`NUMBER`[may parse these numbers and encode them differently to regular text.](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`Here's an example of a user-defined [ Tag](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/struct.Tag.html) for treating integers as Unix timestamps, and a

[that understands them:](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream````
// Define a tag as a constant.
//
// Tags are expected to have unique names.
//
// The rules of our tag are that 64bit unsigned integers that carry it are seconds since
// the Unix epoch.
pub const UNIX_TIMESTAMP: Tag = new;
// Derive `Value` on a type, annotating it with our tag.
//
// We could also implement `Value` manually using `stream.tagged_begin(Some(&UNIX_TIMESTAMP), ..)`.
;
// Here's an example of a `Stream` that understands our tag.
```
The [ Label](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/struct.Label.html) and

[types can also carry a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/struct.Index.html)

`Index`[. An example of a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[you might use on a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[is](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/struct.Label.html)

`Label`[, for labels that hold a valid Rust identifier.](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/tags/constant.VALUE_IDENT.html)

`VALUE_IDENT`### Type system

`sval` has an implicit structural type system based on the sequence of calls a [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) receives, and the values of any

[,](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/struct.Label.html)

`Label`[, or](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/struct.Index.html)

`Index`[on them, with the following exceptions:](https://docs.rs/sval/2.17.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`- Text type does not depend on the composition of fragments, or on their length.
- Binary type does not depend on the composition of fragments, or on their length.
- Sequences are untyped. Their type doesn't depend on the types of their elements, or on their length.
- Maps are untyped. Their type doesn't depend on the types of their keys or values, or on their length.
- Enums holding differently typed variants have the same type.

These rules may be better formalized in the future.

## Ecosystem

`sval` is a general framework with specific serialization formats and utilities provided as external libraries:

- `sval_fmt`
- `sval_json`- `serde`-compatible format.
- `sval_protobuf`
- `sval_serde`- `serde`and- `sval`.
- `sval_buffer`- `Value`
- `sval_flatten`- `#[serde(flatten)]`.
- `sval_nested`- `sval`'s flat- `Stream`- `serde`'s. For types that- `#[derive(Value)]`, the translation is non-allocating.
- `sval_ref`- `Value`- `MyType<'a>`) instead of externally (like- `&'a MyType`).

---

# sval 2.16.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/sval/2.16.0

## What is it?

`sval` is a serialization-only framework for Rust. It has a simple, but expressive design that can express any Rust data structure, plus some it can't yet. It was originally designed as a niche framework for structured logging, targeting serialization to [JSON](https://www.json.org), [protobuf](https://protobuf.dev), and Rust's [Debug-style formatting](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/trait.Debug.html). The project has evolved beyond this point into a fully general and capable framework for introspecting runtime data.

The core of `sval` is the [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) trait. It defines the data model and features of the framework.

`sval` makes a few different API design decisions compared to [, the de-facto choice, to better accommodate the needs of Rust diagnostic frameworks:](https://serde.rs)

`serde`- **Simple API.**The- `Stream`
- `dyn`-friendly.- `Stream`- `dyn`-compatible without intermediate boxing, making it possible to use in no-std environments.
- **Buffer-friendly.**The- `Stream`
- **Borrowing as an optimization.**The- `Stream`- `'sval`, but is also required to accept temporary ones too. This makes it possible to optimize away allocations where possible, but still force them if it's required.
- **Broadly compatible.**- `sval`imposes very few constraints of its own, so it can trivially translate implementations of- `serde::Serialize`- `sval::Value`

`sval`'s data model takes inspiration from [CBOR](https://cbor.io), specifically:

- **Small core.**The base data model of- `sval`is small. The required members of the- `Stream`
- **Extensible tags.**Users can define- *tags*that extend- `sval`'s data model with new semantics. Examples of tags include Rust's- `Some`and- `None`variants, constant-sized arrays, text that doesn't require JSON escaping, and anything else you might need.

## Getting started

This section is a high-level guided tour of `sval`'s design and API. To get started, add `sval` to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "2.16.0"
 = ["derive"]
```
### Serializing values

As a quick example, here's how you can use `sval` to serialize a runtime value as JSON.

First, add [ sval_json](https://docs.rs/sval_json/2.16.0/sval_json/index.html) to your

`Cargo.toml`:```
[]
 = "2.16.0"
 = ["std"]
```
Next, derive the [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/trait.Value.html) trait on the type you want to serialize, including on any other types it uses in its fields:

```
```
Finally, use [ stream_to_string](https://docs.rs/sval_json/2.16.0/sval_json/fn.stream_to_string.html) to serialize an instance of your type as JSON:

```
let my_record = MyRecord ;
// Produces:
//
// {"field_0":1,"field_1":true,"field_2":"some text"}
let json: String = stream_to_string?;
```
### The `Value` trait

The previous example didn't reveal a lot of detail about how `sval` works, only that there's a [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/trait.Value.html) trait involved, and it somehow allows us to convert an instance of the

`MyRecord` struct into a JSON object. Using [, we can peek behind the covers and see what the](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-expand)

`cargo expand``Value` trait does. The previous example expands to something like this:```
```
The [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/trait.Value.html) trait has a single required method,

`stream`, which is responsible for driving an instance of a [with its fields. The](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`[trait defines](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``sval`'s data model and the mechanics of how data is described in it. In this example, the `MyRecord` struct is represented as a *record tuple*, a type that can be either a

*record*with fields named by a

[, or a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/struct.Label.html)

`Label`*tuple*with fields indexed by an

[. Labels and indexes can be annotated with a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/struct.Index.html)

`Index`[which add user-defined semantics to them. In this case, the labels carry the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[tag meaning they're valid Rust identifiers, and the indexes carry the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/tags/constant.VALUE_IDENT.html)

`VALUE_IDENT`[tag meanings they're zero-indexed field offsets. The specific type of](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/tags/constant.VALUE_OFFSET.html)

`VALUE_OFFSET`[can decide whether to treat the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``MyRecord` type as either a record (in the case of JSON) or a tuple (in the case of protobuf), and whether it understands that tags it sees or not.### The `Stream` trait

Something to notice about the [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) API in the expanded

`MyRecord` example is that it is *flat*. The call to

`record_tuple_begin` doesn't return a new type like `serde`'s `serialize_struct` does. The implementor of [is responsible for issuing the correct sequence of](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/trait.Value.html)

`Value`[calls as it works through its structure. The](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`[can then rely on markers like](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``record_tuple_value_begin` and `record_tuple_value_end` to know what position within a value it is without needing to track that state itself. The flat API makes dyn-compatibility and buffering simpler, but makes implementing non-trivial streams more difficult, because you can't rely on recursive to manage state.Recall the way `MyRecord` was converted into JSON earlier:

```
let json: String = stream_to_string?;
```
Internally, [ stream_to_string](https://docs.rs/sval_json/2.16.0/sval_json/fn.stream_to_string.html) uses an instance of

[that writes JSON tokens for each piece of the value it encounters. For example,](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``record_tuple_begin` and `record_tuple_end` will emit the corresponding `{` `}` characters for a JSON object.`sval`'s data model is *layered*. The required methods on [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) represent the base data model that more expressive constructs map down to. Here's what a minimal

[that just formats values in](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``sval`'s base data model looks like:```
;
let my_record = MyRecord ;
// Prints:
//
// [["field_0",1,],["field_1",true,],["field_2","some text",],],
stream;
```
Recall that the `MyRecord` struct mapped to a `record_tuple` in `sval`'s data model. `record_tuple`s in turn are represented in the base data model as a sequence of 2-dimensional sequences where the first element is the field label and the second is its value.

[ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)s aren't limited to just serializing data into interchange formats. They can manipulate or interrogate a value any way it likes. Here's an example of a

[that attempts to extract a specific field of a value as an](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``i32`:```
let my_record = MyRecord ;
assert_eq!;
```
### Streaming text

Strings in `sval` don't need to be streamed in a single call. As an example, say we have a template type like this:

```
;
```
If we wanted to serialize `Template` to a string, we could implement [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/trait.Value.html), handling each literal and property as a separate fragment:

```
```
When streamed as JSON, `Template` would produce something like this:

```
let template = Template;
// Produces:
//
// "some literal text and {x} and more literal text"
let json = stream_to_string?;
```
### Borrowed data

The [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) trait carries a

`'sval` lifetime it can use to accept borrowed text and binary values. Borrowing in `sval` is an optimization. Even if a [uses a concrete](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``'sval` lifetime, it still needs to handle computed values. Here's an example of a [that attempts to extract a borrowed string from a value by making use of the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``'sval` lifetime:```
```
Implementations of [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/trait.Value.html) should provide a

[with borrowed data where possible, and only compute it if it needs to.](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`### Error handling

`sval`'s [ Error](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/struct.Error.html) type doesn't carry any state of its own. It only signals early termination of the

[which may be because its job is done, or because it failed. It's up to the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`[to carry whatever state it needs to provide meaningful errors.](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`## Data model

stream.i64?;
stream.tuple_value_end?;
stream.tuple_value_begin?;
stream.bool?;
stream.tuple_value_end?;
stream.tuple_end?;
stream.enum_end?;
```
```
 a: i64, b: bool }>

stream.enum_begin?;

stream.record_value_begin?;

stream.record_value_end?;

stream.enum_begin?;

#### User-defined tags

`sval` tags, tagged values, records, tuples, enums, and their values can carry a user-defined [ Tag](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/struct.Tag.html) that alters their semantics. A

[may understand a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`[and treat its annotated value differently, or it may ignore them. An example of a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[is](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[, which is for text that encodes an arbitrary-precision decimal floating point number with a standardized format. A](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/tags/constant.NUMBER.html)

`NUMBER`[may parse these numbers and encode them differently to regular text.](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`Here's an example of a user-defined [ Tag](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/struct.Tag.html) for treating integers as Unix timestamps, and a

[that understands them:](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream````
// Define a tag as a constant.
//
// Tags are expected to have unique names.
//
// The rules of our tag are that 64bit unsigned integers that carry it are seconds since
// the Unix epoch.
pub const UNIX_TIMESTAMP: Tag = new;
// Derive `Value` on a type, annotating it with our tag.
//
// We could also implement `Value` manually using `stream.tagged_begin(Some(&UNIX_TIMESTAMP), ..)`.
;
// Here's an example of a `Stream` that understands our tag.
```
The [ Label](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/struct.Label.html) and

[types can also carry a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/struct.Index.html)

`Index`[. An example of a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[you might use on a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[is](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/struct.Label.html)

`Label`[, for labels that hold a valid Rust identifier.](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/tags/constant.VALUE_IDENT.html)

`VALUE_IDENT`### Type system

`sval` has an implicit structural type system based on the sequence of calls a [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) receives, and the values of any

[,](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/struct.Label.html)

`Label`[, or](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/struct.Index.html)

`Index`[on them, with the following exceptions:](https://docs.rs/sval/2.16.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`- Text type does not depend on the composition of fragments, or on their length.
- Binary type does not depend on the composition of fragments, or on their length.
- Sequences are untyped. Their type doesn't depend on the types of their elements, or on their length.
- Maps are untyped. Their type doesn't depend on the types of their keys or values, or on their length.
- Enums holding differently typed variants have the same type.

These rules may be better formalized in the future.

## Ecosystem

`sval` is a general framework with specific serialization formats and utilities provided as external libraries:

- `sval_fmt`
- `sval_json`- `serde`-compatible format.
- `sval_protobuf`
- `sval_serde`- `serde`and- `sval`.
- `sval_buffer`- `Value`
- `sval_flatten`- `#[serde(flatten)]`.
- `sval_nested`- `sval`'s flat- `Stream`- `serde`'s. For types that- `#[derive(Value)]`, the translation is non-allocating.
- `sval_ref`- `Value`- `MyType<'a>`) instead of externally (like- `&'a MyType`).

# sval 2.15.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/sval/2.15.0

`sval`: Streaming, structured values

## What is it?

`sval` is a serialization-only framework for Rust. It has a simple, but expressive design that can express any Rust data structure, plus some it can't yet. It was originally designed as a niche framework for structured logging, targeting serialization to [JSON]([https://www.json.org](https://www.json.org), [protobuf](https://protobuf.dev), and Rust's [Debug-style formatting](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/trait.Debug.html). The project has evolved beyond this point into a fully general and capable framework for introspecting runtime data.

The core of `sval` is the [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.15.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) trait. It defines the data model and features of the framework.

`sval` makes a few different API design decisions compared to [, the de-facto choice, to better accommodate the needs of Rust diagnostic frameworks:](https://serde.rs)

`serde`- **Simple API.**The- `Stream`
- `dyn`-friendly.- `Stream`- `dyn`-compatible without intermediate boxing, making it possible to use in no-std environments.
- **Buffer-friendly.**The- `Stream`
- **Borrowing as an optimization.**The- `Stream`- `'sval`, but is also required to accept temporary ones too. This makes it possible to optimize away allocations where possible, but still force them if it's required.
- **Broadly compatible.**- `sval`imposes very few constraints of its own, so it can trivially translate implementations of- `serde::Serialize`- `sval::Value`

`sval`'s data model takes inspiration from [CBOR](https://cbor.io), specifically:

- **Small core.**The base data model of- `sval`is small. The required members of the- `Stream`
- **Extensible tags.**Users can define- *tags*that extend- `sval`'s data model with new semantics. Examples of tags include Rust's- `Some`and- `None`variants, constant-sized arrays, text that doesn't require JSON escaping, and anything else you might need.

## Getting started

This section is a high-level guided tour of `sval`'s design and API. To get started, add `sval` to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "2.15.0"
 = ["derive"]
```
### Serializing values

As a quick example, here's how you can use `sval` to serialize a runtime value as JSON.

First, add [ sval_json](https://docs.rs/sval_json/2.15.0/sval_json/index.html) to your

`Cargo.toml`:```
[]
 = "2.15.0"
 = ["std"]
```
Next, derive the [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.15.0/sval/trait.Value.html) trait on the type you want to serialize, including on any other types it uses in its fields:

```
```
Finally, use [ stream_to_string](https://docs.rs/sval_json/2.15.0/sval_json/fn.stream_to_string.html) to serialize an instance of your type as JSON:

```
let my_record = MyRecord ;
// Produces:
//
// {"field_0":1,"field_1":true,"field_2":"some text"}
let json: String = stream_to_string?;
```
### The `Value` trait

The previous example didn't reveal a lot of detail about how `sval` works, only that there's a [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.15.0/sval/trait.Value.html) trait involved, and it somehow allows us to convert an instance of the

`MyRecord` struct into a JSON object. Using [, we can peek behind the covers and see what the](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-expand)

`cargo expand``Value` trait does. The previous example expands to something like this:```
```
The [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.15.0/sval/trait.Value.html) trait has a single required method,

`stream`, which is responsible for driving an instance of a [with its fields. The](https://docs.rs/sval/2.15.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`[trait defines](https://docs.rs/sval/2.15.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``sval`'s data model and the mechanics of how data is described in it. In this example, the `MyRecord` struct is represented as a *record tuple*, a type that can be either a

*record*with fields named by a

[, or a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.15.0/sval/struct.Label.html)

`Label`*tuple*with fields indexed by an

[. Labels and indexes can be annotated with a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.15.0/sval/struct.Index.html)

`Index`[which add user-defined semantics to them. In this case, the labels carry the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.15.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[tag meaning they're valid Rust identifiers, and the indexes carry the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.15.0/sval/tags/constant.VALUE_IDENT.html)

`VALUE_IDENT`[tag meanings they're zero-indexed field offsets. The specific type of](https://docs.rs/sval/2.15.0/sval/tags/constant.VALUE_OFFSET.html)

`VALUE_OFFSET`[can decide whether to treat the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.15.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``MyRecord` type as either a record (in the case of JSON) or a tuple (in the case of protobuf), and whether it understands that tags it sees or not.### The `Stream` trait

Something to notice about the [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.15.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) API in the expanded

`MyRecord` example is that it is *flat*. The call to

`record_tuple_begin` doesn't return a new type like `serde`'s `struct_begin` does. The implementor of [is responsible for issuing the correct sequence of](https://docs.rs/sval/2.15.0/sval/trait.Value.html)

`Value`[calls as it works through its structure. The](https://docs.rs/sval/2.15.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`[can then rely on markers like](https://docs.rs/sval/2.15.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``record_tuple_value_begin` and `record_tuple_value_end` to know what position within a value it is without needing to track that state itself. The flat API makes dyn-compatibility and buffering simpler, but makes implementing non-trivial streams more difficult, because you can't rely on recursive to manage state.Recall the way `MyRecord` was converted into JSON earlier:

```
let json: String = stream_to_string?;
```
Internally, [ stream_to_string](https://docs.rs/sval_json/2.15.0/sval_json/fn.stream_to_string.html) uses an instance of

[that writes JSON tokens for each piece of the value it encounters. For example,](https://docs.rs/sval/2.15.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``record_tuple_begin` and `record_tuple_end` will emit the corresponding `{` `}` characters for a JSON object.`sval`'s data model is *layered*. The required methods on [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.15.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) represent the base data model that more expressive constructs map down to. Here's what a minimal

[that just formats values in](https://docs.rs/sval/2.15.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``sval`'s base data model looks like:```
;
let my_record = MyRecord ;
// Prints:
//
// [["field_0",1,],["field_1",true,],["field_2","some text",],],
stream;
```
Recall that the `MyRecord` struct mapped to a `record_tuple` in `sval`'s data model. `record_tuple`s in turn are represented in the base data model as a sequence of 2-dimensional sequences where the first element is the field label and the second is its value.

[ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.15.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)s aren't limited to just serializing data into interchange formats. They can manipulate or interrogate a value any way it likes. Here's an example of a

[that attempts to extract a specific field of a value as an](https://docs.rs/sval/2.15.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``i32`:```
let my_record = MyRecord ;
assert_eq!;
```
### Streaming text

Strings in `sval` don't need to be streamed in a single call. As an example, say we have a template type like this:

```
;
```
If we wanted to serialize `Template` to a string, we could implement [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.15.0/sval/trait.Value.html), handling each literal and property as a separate fragment:

```
```
When streamed as JSON, `Template` would produce something like this:

```
let template = Template;
// Produces:
//
// "some literal text and {x} and more literal text"
let json = stream_to_string?;
```
### Borrowed data

The [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.15.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) trait carries a

`'sval` lifetime it can use to accept borrowed text and binary values. Borrowing in `sval` is an optimization. Even if a [uses a concrete](https://docs.rs/sval/2.15.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``'sval` lifetime, it still needs to handle computed values. Here's an example of a [that attempts to extract a borrowed string from a value by making use of the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.15.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``'sval` lifetime:```
```
Implementations of [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.15.0/sval/trait.Value.html) should provide a

[with borrowed data where possible, and only compute it if it needs to.](https://docs.rs/sval/2.15.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`### Error handling

`sval`'s [ Error](https://docs.rs/sval/2.15.0/sval/struct.Error.html) type doesn't carry any state of its own. It only signals early termination of the

[which may be because its job is done, or because it failed. It's up to the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.15.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`[to carry whatever state it needs to provide meaningful errors.](https://docs.rs/sval/2.15.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`## Data model

This section descibes `sval`'s data model in detail using examples in Rust syntax. Some types in `sval`'s model aren't representable in Rust yet, so they use pseudo syntax.

stream.seq_end?;

Note that Rust arrays are homogeneous, but `sval` sequences are heterogeneous.

# sval 2.14.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/sval/2.14.1

`sval`: Streaming, structured values

`sval` is a lightweight serialization-only framework that treats values like a flat stream of tokens.
It's well suited to self-describing text formats like JSON.

## How is this different from `serde`?

`serde` is the de-facto serialization framework for Rust and is well suited to the majority of
use cases. `sval` is like a light blend of `serde::ser` and `serde::de` that is smaller in scope.
It makes a few key different design decisions than `serde` that make it effective for working with
self-describing formats:

- The API is flat rather than using recursion to stream nested datastructures.
- All values with dynamic sizes, including text strings, can be streamed in multiple calls.
- Borrowing is an optional optimization.
- The core data model is small, with tags for extensibility.

# Data-model

- Values:
- `null`: the absence of any other meaningful value.
- Booleans: `true`and`false`.
- Text strings: stream of UTF8-encoded bytes.
- Binary strings: stream of arbtirary bytes.
- Numbers:
- Integers: `u8`-`u128`,`i8`-`i128`.
- Binary floating point: `f32`-`f64`.

- Integers:
- Maps: heterogeneous collection of key-value pairs.
- Sequences: heterogeneous collection of values.
- Tags: out-of-band type hints.
- Tagged values: a tag associated with a value.
- Records: tagged maps where keys are well-known labels.
- Tuples: tagged sequences.
- Enums: tagged variants, where variants are enums, tags, tagged values, records, or tuples.

`sval` includes built-in tags that extend its data-model with some common datatypes:

- Rust primitives:
- `()`.
- `Option<T>`.

- Arbitrary-precision decimal floating point numbers.

Other built-in tags may be added in the future. Libraries may also define their own tags.

## Current status

This project has a complete and stable API, but isn't well documented yet.

---

# sval 2.8.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/sval/2.8.0

`sval`: Streaming, structured values

`sval` is a lightweight serialization-only framework that treats values like a flat stream of tokens.
It's well suited to self-describing text formats like JSON.

## How is this different from `serde`?

`serde` is the de-facto serialization framework for Rust and is well suited to the majority of
use cases. `sval` is like a light blend of `serde::ser` and `serde::de` that is smaller in scope.
It makes a few key different design decisions than `serde` that make it effective for working with
self-describing formats:

- The API is flat rather than using recursion to stream nested datastructures.
- All values with dynamic sizes, including text strings, can be streamed in multiple calls.
- Borrowing is an optional optimization.
- The core data model is small, with tags for extensibility.

# Data-model

- Values:
- `null`: the absence of any other meaningful value.
- Booleans: `true`and`false`.
- Text strings: stream of UTF8-encoded bytes.
- Binary strings: stream of arbtirary bytes.
- Numbers:
- Integers: `u8`-`u128`,`i8`-`i128`.
- Binary floating point: `f32`-`f64`.

- Integers:
- Maps: heterogeneous collection of key-value pairs.
- Sequences: heterogeneous collection of values.
- Tags: out-of-band type hints.
- Tagged values: a tag associated with a value.
- Records: tagged maps where keys are well-known labels.
- Tuples: tagged sequences.
- Enums: tagged variants, where variants are enums, tags, tagged values, records, or tuples.

`sval` includes built-in tags that extend its data-model with some common datatypes:

- Rust primitives:
- `()`.
- `Option<T>`.

- Arbitrary-precision decimal floating point numbers.

Other built-in tags may be added in the future. Libraries may also define their own tags.

## Current status

This project has a complete and stable API, but isn't well documented yet.

---

# sval 2.0.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/sval/2.0.2

`sval`: Streaming, structured values

`sval` is a lightweight serialization-only framework that treats values like a flat stream of tokens.
It's well suited to self-describing text formats like JSON.

## How is this different from `serde`?

`serde` is the de-facto serialization framework for Rust and is well suited to the majority of
use cases. `sval` is like a light blend of `serde::ser` and `serde::de` that is smaller in scope.
It makes a few key different design decisions than `serde` that make it effective for working with
self-describing formats:

- The API is flat rather than using recursion to stream nested datastructures.
- All values with dynamic sizes, including text strings, can be streamed in multiple calls.
- Borrowing is an optional optimization.
- The core data model is small, with tags for extensibility.

# Data-model

- Values:
- `null`: the absence of any other meaningful value.
- Booleans: `true`and`false`.
- Text strings: stream of UTF8-encoded bytes.
- Binary strings: stream of arbtirary bytes.
- Numbers:
- Integers: `u8`-`u128`,`i8`-`i128`.
- Binary floating point: `f32`-`f64`.

- Integers:
- Maps: heterogeneous collection of key-value pairs.
- Sequences: heterogeneous collection of values.
- Tags: out-of-band type hints.
- Tagged values: a tag associated with a value.
- Records: tagged maps where keys are well-known labels.
- Tuples: tagged sequences.
- Enums: tagged variants, where variants are enums, tags, tagged values, records, or tuples.

`sval` includes built-in tags that extend its data-model with some common datatypes:

- Rust primitives:
- `()`.
- `Option<T>`.

- Arbitrary-precision decimal floating point numbers.

Other built-in tags may be added in the future. Libraries may also define their own tags.

## Current status

This project has a complete and stable API, but isn't well documented yet.

---

# sval 1.0.0-alpha.5 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/sval/1.0.0-alpha.5

`sval`

A lightweight, no-std, object-safe, serialization-only API for structured values with `serde` and `std::fmt` support.

Producers of structured values use the `value` module. Consumers of structured values use the `stream` module.

`sval` offers a JSON-like data model, which is more limiting than `serde`'s, but capable enough to represent Rust data-structures in one form or another.

This library is designed to plug a no-std-object-safe sized hole in Rust's current serialization ecosystem. The driving use-case is structured logging, where individual events are typically small, and there's no complete schema that can tie values in any one event to values in another.

`sval_json` and `sval_derive` are mostly pilfered from dtolnay's [excellent  miniserde project](https://github.com/dtolnay/miniserde).

# Supported formats

- [JSON](https://crates.io/crates/sval_json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.

# Minimum `rustc`

This library requires Rust `1.31.0`.

# See also

# Cargo features

`sval` has the following optional features that can be enabled in your `Cargo.toml`:

- `std`: assume- `std`is available and add support for- `std`types. Implies- `alloc`.
- `alloc`: assume a global allocator is available.
- `derive`: add support for- `#[derive(Value)]`.
- `serde`: enable integration with major versions of- `serde`. Some implementations of- `sval::Value`may not be representable without the- `alloc`feature.- `serde1`: enable integration with just the- `1.x`version of- `serde`. Any future versions of- `serde`will also receive their own feature.

- `fmt`: support converting any- `Value`into a- `Debug`.
- `arbitrary-depth`: support stateful values with any depth. Implies- `alloc`.
- `test`: add helpers for testing implementations of- `Value`. Implies- `std`. You should avoid using this feature outside of- `dev-dependencies`.

# How to use it

Add `sval` to your crate dependencies:

```
[]
 = "1.0.0-alpha.5"
```
## To support my data-structures

Simple struct-like data-structures can derive `sval::Value`:

```
[]
 = ["derive"]
```
```
extern crate sval;
```
Other data-structures can implement `sval::Value` manually:

```
use ;
;
```
## To format my data

The `sval_json` crate can format any `sval::Value` as JSON:

```
[]
 = "1.0.0-alpha.5"
 = ["std"]
```
```
let my_json = to_string?;
```
## To integrate with `serde`

`sval` has out-of-the-box `serde` integration between `sval::Value`s and `serde::Serialize`s. Add the `serde` feature to `sval` to enable it:

```
[]
 = ["serde"]
```
Use the `to_serialize` function to turn any `sval::Value` into a `serde::Serialize`:

```
let my_serialize = to_serialize;
```
Use the `to_value` function to turn any `serde::Serialize` into a `sval::Value`:

```
let my_value = to_value;
```
When the `serde` feature is available, structures that already derive `Serialize` can also always derive `Value`. The `Value` implementation will behave the same as `Serialize`:

```
```
## To integrate with `std::fmt`

`sval` can provide a compatible `Debug` implementation for any `sval::Value`. Add the `fmt` feature to `sval` to enable it:

```
[]
 = ["fmt"]
```
Use the `to_debug` function to turn any `sval::Value` into a `std::fmt::Debug`:

```
```

---

- `test`: add helpers for testing implementations of- `Value`. Implies- `std`. You should avoid using this feature outside of- `dev-dependencies`.

# sval 0.5.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/sval/0.5.0

`sval`

A lightweight, no-std, object-safe, serialization-only API for structured values with `serde` and `std::fmt` support.

Producers of structured values use the `value` module. Consumers of structured values use the `stream` module.

`sval` offers a JSON-like data model, which is more limiting than `serde`'s, but capable enough to represent Rust data-structures in one form or another.

This library is designed to plug a no-std-object-safe sized hole in Rust's current serialization ecosystem. The driving use-case is structured logging, where individual events are typically small, and there's no complete schema that can tie values in any one event to values in another.

`sval_json` and `sval_derive` are mostly pilfered from dtolnay's [excellent  miniserde project](https://github.com/dtolnay/miniserde).

# Supported formats

- [JSON](https://crates.io/crates/sval_json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.

# Minimum `rustc`

This library requires Rust `1.31.0`.

# See also

# Cargo features

`sval` has the following optional features that can be enabled in your `Cargo.toml`:

- `std`: assume- `std`is available and add support for- `std`types. Implies- `alloc`.
- `alloc`: assume a global allocator is available.
- `derive`: add support for- `#[derive(Value)]`.
- `serde`: enable integration with- `serde`. Some implementations of- `sval::Value`may not be representable without the- `alloc`feature.
- `fmt`: support converting any- `Value`into a- `Debug`.
- `arbitrary-depth`: support stateful values with any depth. Implies- `alloc`.
- `test`: add helpers for testing implementations of- `Value`. Implies- `std`. You should avoid using this feature outside of- `dev-dependencies`.

# How to use it

Add `sval` to your crate dependencies:

```

## To support my data-structures

```
Other data-structures can implement `sval::Value` manually:

```

;
```

```
[]
 = "0.5.0"
 = ["std"]
```
```

```
## To integrate with `serde`

```
[]

```

```

```

`sval`

A lightweight, no-std, object-safe, serialization-only API for structured values with `serde` and `std::fmt` support.

Producers of structured values use the `value` module. Consumers of structured values use the `stream` module.

`sval` offers a JSON-like data model, which is more limiting than `serde`'s, but capable enough to represent Rust data-structures in one form or another.

This library is designed to plug a no-std-object-safe sized hole in Rust's current serialization ecosystem. The driving use-case is structured logging, where individual events are typically small, and there's no complete schema that can tie values in any one event to values in another.

`sval_json` and `sval_derive` are mostly pilfered from dtolnay's [excellent  miniserde project](https://github.com/dtolnay/miniserde).

`sval_json` and `sval_derive` are mostly pilfered from dtolnay's [excellent  miniserde project](https://github.com/dtolnay/miniserde).

# Supported formats

- [JSON](https://crates.io/crates/sval_json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.

# Minimum `rustc`

This library requires Rust `1.31.0`.

# See also

# Cargo features

`sval` has the following optional features that can be enabled in your `Cargo.toml`:

- `std`: assume- `std`is available and add support for- `std`types.
- `derive`: add support for- `#[derive(Value)]`.
- `serde`: enable integration with- `serde`.
- `fmt`: support converting any- `Value`into a- `Debug`.
- `arbitrary-depth`: support stateful values with any depth.
- `test`: add helpers for testing implementations of- `Value`.

# How to use it

Add `sval` to your crate dependencies:

```
[]
 = "0.4.1"
```
## To support my data-structures

Simple struct-like data-structures can derive `sval::Value`:

```
[]
 = ["derive"]
```
```
extern crate sval;
```
Other data-structures can implement `sval::Value` manually:

```
use ;
;
```
## To format my data

The `sval_json` crate can format any `sval::Value` as JSON:

```
[]
 = "0.4.1"
 = ["std"]
```
```
let my_json = to_string?;
```
## To integrate with `serde`

`sval` has out-of-the-box `serde` integration between `sval::Value`s and `serde::Serialize`s. Add the `serde` feature to `sval` to enable it:

```
[]
 = ["serde"]
```
Use the `to_serialize` function to turn any `sval::Value` into a `serde::Serialize`:

```
let my_serialize = to_serialize;
```
Use the `to_value` function to turn any `serde::Serialize` into a `sval::Value`:

```
let my_value = to_value;
```
When the `serde` feature is available, structures that already derive `Serialize` can also always derive `Value`. The `Value` implementation will behave the same as `Serialize`:

```
```
## To integrate with `std::fmt`

`sval` can provide a compatible `Debug` implementation for any `sval::Value`. Add the `fmt` feature to `sval` to enable it:

```
[]
 = ["fmt"]
```
Use the `to_debug` function to turn any `sval::Value` into a `std::fmt::Debug`:

```
```

---

`sval`

A lightweight, no-std, object-safe, serialization-only API for structured values with `serde` and `std::fmt` support.

# Minimum `rustc`

This library requires Rust `1.31.0`.

# See also

# Crate features

- `std`: assume- `std`is available and add support for- `std`types.
- `derive`: add support for- `#[derive(Value)]`.
- `serde`: enable integration with- `serde`.
- `arbitrary-depth`: support stateful values with any depth.
- `test`: add helpers for testing implementations of- `Value`.

# How to use it

Add `sval` to your crate dependencies:

```
[]
 = "0.1.1"
```

Simple struct-like datastructures can derive `sval::Value`:

```
[]
 = ["derive"]
```
```

```
Other datastructures can implement `sval::Value` manually:

```

;
```

```
[]
 = "0.1.1"
 = ["std"]
```
```

```
## To integrate with `serde`

`sval` has out-of-the-box `serde` integration between `sval::Value`s and `serde::Serialize`s. Add the `serde` feature to `sval` to enable it:

```
[]
 = ["serde"]
```
Use the `to_serialize` function to turn any `sval::Value` into a `serde::Serialize`:

```

```

```

```

# sval - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sval

## Expand description

Structured, streaming values.

`sval` is a serialization framework that treats data as a flat stream of tokens.
The source of that data could be some Rust object or parsed from some encoding.
It’s well suited to self-describing, text-based formats like JSON.

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting started

For a complete introduction, see [the project readme](https://github.com/sval-rs/sval).

Add `sval` to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies.sval]
version = "2.20.0"
```
By default, `sval` doesn’t depend on Rust’s standard library or integrate with its collection types.
To include them, add the `alloc` or `std` Cargo features:

```
[dependencies.sval]
version = "2.20.0"
features = ["std"]
```
`sval` provides procedural macros for deriving its traits.
Add the `derive` Cargo feature to enable them:

```
[dependencies.sval]
version = "2.20.0"
features = ["derive"]
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-value-trait)The `Value` trait

[ Value](https://docs.rs/trait.Value.html) is a trait for data types to implement that surfaces their structure through visitors called

*streams*.

`Value` is like `serde`’s `Serialize`. It can also be used like `serde`’s `Deserialize`.Many standard types in Rust implement the `Value` trait. It can be derived on your own types using the `sval_derive` library.

[§](https://docs.rs#the-stream-trait)The `Stream` trait

[ Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.Stream.html) is a trait for data formats and visitors to implement that observes the structure of

*values*.

`Stream` is like `serde`’s `Serializer`. It can also be used like `serde`’s `Deserializer`.[§](https://docs.rs#data-model)Data-model

`sval`’s data-model is defined by the [ Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.Stream.html) trait. It includes:

- Null
- Booleans (`true`,`false`)
- Text blobs
- Binary blobs
- Integers (`u8`-`u128`,`i8`-`i128`)
- Binary floating points (`f32`-`f64`)
- Sequences
- Maps
- Tags
- Tagged values
- Records
- Tuples
- Enums

[§](https://docs.rs#tags)Tags

[ Tag](https://docs.rs/struct.Tag.html) is a type for extending

`sval`’s data-model with new kinds of values.
Rust’s own `()` and `Option<T>` types are expressed as tags.
Other examples of tags include text that encodes RFC3339 timestamps or RFC4122 UUIDs.The [ tags](https://docs.rs/tags/index.html) module contains built-in tags.
Other libraries may define their own tags too.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [default_](https://docs.rs/default_stream/index.html)- stream
- Default method implementations for `Stream`
- [default_](https://docs.rs/default_value/index.html)- value
- Default method implementations for `Value`
- [tags](https://docs.rs/tags/index.html)
- Built-in tags for fundamental types.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Binary](https://docs.rs/struct.BinaryArray.html)- Array
- An adapter that streams a slice of 8bit unsigned integers as binary with a fixed size.
- [Binary](https://docs.rs/struct.BinarySlice.html)- Slice
- An adapter that streams a slice of 8bit unsigned integers as binary.
- [Display](https://docs.rs/struct.Display.html)
- Adapt a `fmt::Display``sval::Value`].
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- An error encountered while streaming a value.
- [Index](https://docs.rs/struct.Index.html)
- The index of a value in its parent context.
- [Label](https://docs.rs/struct.Label.html)
- A textual label for some value.
- [MapSlice](https://docs.rs/struct.MapSlice.html)
- An adapter that streams a slice of key-value pairs as a map.
- [Null](https://docs.rs/struct.Null.html)
- The absence of any meaningful value.
- [Tag](https://docs.rs/struct.Tag.html)
- A type tag for a value.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [error](https://docs.rs/fn.error.html)
- A streaming result with a generic failure.
- [stream](https://docs.rs/fn.stream.html)
- Stream a value through a stream.
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_computed.html)- computed
- Stream a value through a stream with an arbitrarily short lifetime.
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_display.html)- display
- Stream a `fmt::Display``Stream`
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_display_fragments.html)- display_ - fragments
- Stream a `fmt::Display``Stream``Stream::text_begin``Stream::text_end`
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_number.html)- number
- Stream an arbitrary precision number conforming to `tags::NUMBER``fmt::Display`

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- A generic streaming result.

# Serialize in serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/latest/serde/trait.Serialize.html

```
pub trait Serialize {
    // Required method
    fn
```
[serialize](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serialize)<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<S::[Ok](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Ok), S::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>
       where S: [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html);
}## Expand description

A **data structure** that can be serialized into any data format supported
by Serde.

Serde provides `Serialize` implementations for many Rust primitive and
standard library types. The complete list is [here](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html). All of
these can be serialized using Serde out of the box.

Additionally, Serde provides a procedural macro called [ serde_derive](https://crates.io/crates/serde_derive) to
automatically generate

`Serialize` implementations for structs and enums in
your program. See the [derive section of the manual](https://serde.rs/derive.html)for how to use this.

In rare cases it may be necessary to implement `Serialize` manually for some
type in your program. See the [Implementing  Serialize](https://serde.rs/impl-serialize.html) section of the
manual for more about this.

Third-party crates may provide `Serialize` implementations for types that
they expose. For example the [ linked-hash-map](https://crates.io/crates/linked-hash-map) crate provides a

[type that is serializable by Serde because the crate provides an implementation of](https://docs.rs/linked-hash-map/*/linked_hash_map/struct.LinkedHashMap.html)

`LinkedHashMap<K, V>``Serialize` for it.## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Serialize this value into the given Serde serializer.

See the [Implementing  Serialize](https://serde.rs/impl-serialize.html) section of the manual for more
information about how to implement this method.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeStruct, Serializer};
struct Person {
    name: String,
    age: u8,
    phones: Vec<String>,
}
// This is what #[derive(Serialize)] would generate.
impl Serialize for Person {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut s = serializer.serialize_struct("Person", 3)?;
        s.serialize_field("name", &self.name)?;
        s.serialize_field("age", &self.age)?;
        s.serialize_field("phones", &self.phones)?;
        s.end()
    }
}
```
## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

## Implementations on Foreign Types[§](https://docs.rs#foreign-impls)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/impls.rs.html#397-402)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Serialize-for-(T,))### impl<T> [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html) for [(T₁, T₂, …, Tₙ)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.tuple.html#trait-implementations-1)

This trait is implemented for tuples up to 16 items long.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/impls.rs.html#397-402)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Serialize-for-(T,))

### impl<T> [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html) for [(T₁, T₂, …, Tₙ)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.tuple.html#trait-implementations-1)

This trait is implemented for tuples up to 16 items long.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/impls.rs.html#492-504)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Serialize-for-Rc%3CT%3E)Available on **crate feature **`rc` and (crate features `std` or `alloc`) only.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/impls.rs.html#492-504)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Serialize-for-Rc%3CT%3E)

**crate feature**only.

`rc` and (crate features `std` or `alloc`)Serializing a data structure containing `Rc` will serialize a copy of
the contents of the `Rc` each time the `Rc` is referenced within the
data structure. Serialization will not attempt to deduplicate these
repeated data.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/impls.rs.html#506-518)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Serialize-for-Arc%3CT%3E)Available on **crate feature **`rc` and (crate features `std` or `alloc`) only.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/impls.rs.html#506-518)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Serialize-for-Arc%3CT%3E)

**crate feature**only.

`rc` and (crate features `std` or `alloc`)Serializing a data structure containing `Arc` will serialize a copy of
the contents of the `Arc` each time the `Arc` is referenced within the
data structure. Serialization will not attempt to deduplicate these
repeated data.

# sval_json - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sval_json/2.20.0/sval_json/index.html

## Expand description

JSON support for `sval`.

Values are serialized in a `serde`-compatible way.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [tags](https://docs.rs/tags/index.html)
- Tags for JSON-specific types.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

# sval_protobuf - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sval_protobuf/latest/sval_protobuf/

## Expand description

[protobuf](https://protobuf.dev/) support for `sval`.

This library implements a binary encoding for `sval::Value`s that’s compatible with the
protobuf [wire format](https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/encoding/).

This library doesn’t depend on `protoc` or any code generation tools; any implementation of
`sval::Value` can be encoded. You can use it in cases where standard code generation is either
impractical or produces undesirable results. It supports some more niche use-cases like embedding
already encoded messages into others without needing to parse them first.

This library only supports encoding.

[§](https://docs.rs#specifics)Specifics

This section uses [protoscope](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protoscope) syntax for
encoded messages.

[§](https://docs.rs#messages)Messages

If you `#[derive(Value)]`, your structs are encoded as messages:

```
#[derive(Value)]
pub struct Record<'a> {
    id: i32,
    title: &'a str,
    data: &'a str,
}
Record {
    id: 42,
    title: "My Message",
    data: "Some amazing content",
}
```
```
1: 42
2: {"My Message"}
3: {"Some amazing content"}
```
Specify an `#[sval(index)]` on fields to set the field number explicitly:

```
#[derive(Value)]
pub struct ManuallyIndexed<'a> {
    #[sval(index = 3)]
    id: i32,
    #[sval(index = 7)]
    title: &'a str,
}
ManuallyIndexed {
    id: 42,
    title: "My Message",
}
```
```
3: 42
7: {"My Message"}
```
Anonymous tuples are also messages:

```
(
    42,
    "My Message",
    "Some amazing content",
)
```
```
1: 42
2: {"My Message"}
3: {"Some amazing content"}
```
128bit numbers are always encoded as a 16 byte buffer with the little-endian bytes of the value.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use crate::buf::`- [Capacity](https://docs.rs/buf/struct.Capacity.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Proto](https://docs.rs/struct.ProtoBufStream.html)- BufStream
- An `sval::Stream`
- [Proto](https://docs.rs/struct.ProtoBufStreamReusable.html)- BufStream - Reusable
- The re-usable internals of a `ProtoBufStream`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_to_protobuf.html)- to_ - protobuf
- Encode a value to the protobuf wire format.

# sval_serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sval_serde/2.20.0/sval_serde/index.html

## Expand description

Treat any [ sval::Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sval/value/trait.Value.html) as a [

`serde::Serialize`].This crate provides `ToSerialize`, a wrapper around any `sval::Value`
that forwards it through `serde`.

[§](https://docs.rs#buffering)Buffering

Add the `alloc` feature to enable buffering for values that need it.

Types that derive [ sval::Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sval/value/trait.Value.html) automatically can be streamed through

`serde` without requiring any buffering. Types that manually stream
text across multiple fragments, or nested fields without recursing through
`Stream::value` will need to be buffered.Without the `alloc` feature, any values that require buffering will instead
produce errors during serialization.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [ToSerialize](https://docs.rs/struct.ToSerialize.html)
- Adapt an `sval::Value``serde_core::Serialize`
- [ToValue](https://docs.rs/struct.ToValue.html)
- Adapt a `serde_core::Serialize``sval::Value`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [serialize](https://docs.rs/fn.serialize.html)
- Serialize an `sval::Value``serde_core::Serializer`
- [stream](https://docs.rs/fn.stream.html)
- Stream a `serde_core::Serialize``sval::Stream`

# sval_buffer - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sval_buffer/2.20.0/sval_buffer/index.html

## Expand description

Buffering support for `sval`.

This crate provides the [ ValueBuf](https://docs.rs/struct.ValueBuf.html) type, which can buffer a flat
stream of data into a tree of borrowed values.

Some functionality requires the `alloc` Cargo feature to be enabled.
Rather than conditionally compile these methods, this library stubs
out functionality when an allocator isn’t available.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Binary](https://docs.rs/struct.BinaryBuf.html)- Buf
- Buffer binary fragments into a single contiguous slice.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- An error encountered buffering data.
- [TextBuf](https://docs.rs/struct.TextBuf.html)
- Buffer text fragments into a single contiguous string.
- [Value](https://docs.rs/struct.Value.html)
- An immutable buffered value.
- [Value](https://docs.rs/struct.ValueBuf.html)- Buf
- Buffer arbitrary values into a tree-like structure.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_to_value.html)- to_ - value
- Buffer a value.
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_to_value_owned.html)- to_ - value_ - owned
- Buffer an owned value.

# sval_flatten - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sval_flatten/2.20.0/sval_flatten/index.html

## Expand description

Flatten nested values when streaming.

This library is like the standard library’s `Iterator::flatten` method, but for `sval::Stream`s.
Given a value, it will flatten its nested values onto a parent structure. It supports flattening
any combination of map, sequence, record, or tuple onto any other.

If you’re using `sval_derive`, you can use the `#[flatten]` attribute on a field.

[§](https://docs.rs#specifics)Specifics

Flattening unwraps containers and translates their values into the form needed by their parent. The following types can be flattened:

- maps
- sequences
- records
- tuples

Any other type, including primitives like tags, booleans, and text will be ignored if flattened.

[§](https://docs.rs#maps)Maps

- **maps**: keys are passed through directly, even if they’re complex values like other maps.
- **sequences**: keys are the stringified offset of sequence values.
- **records**: keys are the label of record values.
- **tuples**: keys are the stringified index of tuple values.

[§](https://docs.rs#sequences)Sequences

- **maps**: map keys are ignored; only map values are flattened.
- **sequences**: sequence values are passed through directly.
- **records**: record values are passed through directly.
- **tuples**: tuple values are passed through directly.

[§](https://docs.rs#records)Records

- **maps**: map keys are stringified into labels. For complex values like other maps each nested value is stringified and concatenated together.
- **sequences**: labels are the stringified offset of sequence values.
- **records**: labels are passed through directly.
- **tuples**: labels are the stringified index of tuple values.

[§](https://docs.rs#tuples)Tuples

- **maps**: map keys are ignored; only map values are flattened.
- **sequences**: indexes are the offset of sequence values.
- **records**: indexes are the offset of record values.
- **tuples**: tuple values are passed through directly.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Flatten](https://docs.rs/struct.FlattenToMap.html)- ToMap
- A stream that flattens the fields of a value onto a map.
- [Flatten](https://docs.rs/struct.FlattenToRecord.html)- ToRecord
- A stream that flattens the fields of a value onto a record.
- [Flatten](https://docs.rs/struct.FlattenToRecordTuple.html)- ToRecord - Tuple
- A stream that flattens the fields of a value onto a record or tuple.
- [Flatten](https://docs.rs/struct.FlattenToSeq.html)- ToSeq
- A stream that flattens the fields of a value onto a sequence.
- [Flatten](https://docs.rs/struct.FlattenToTuple.html)- ToTuple
- A stream that flattens the fields of a value onto a tuple.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [flatten_](https://docs.rs/fn.flatten_to_map.html)- to_ - map
- Flatten the fields of a value onto a map.
- [flatten_](https://docs.rs/fn.flatten_to_record.html)- to_ - record
- Flatten the fields of a value onto a record.
- [flatten_](https://docs.rs/fn.flatten_to_record_tuple.html)- to_ - record_ - tuple
- Flatten the fields of a value onto a record or tuple.
- [flatten_](https://docs.rs/fn.flatten_to_seq.html)- to_ - seq
- Flatten the fields of a value onto a sequence.
- [flatten_](https://docs.rs/fn.flatten_to_tuple.html)- to_ - tuple
- Flatten the fields of a value onto a tuple.

# sval_nested - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sval_nested/2.20.0/sval_nested/index.html

## Expand description

A variant of [ sval::Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sval/stream/trait.Stream.html) for cases where a recursive API is needed.

[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

Streaming via `sval_nested` will discard any [ sval::Stream::tag_hint](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sval/stream/trait.Stream.html#method.tag_hint)s.

`sval` allows tag hints to
appear anywhere in a stream, but this library enforces a stricter lifecycle, making those hints unreliable.## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [default_](https://docs.rs/default_stream/index.html)- stream
- Default method implementations for the `Stream`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- An error encountered buffering data.

- Adapt an `sval::Value``ValueRef`

- A stream for a map.
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.StreamRecord.html)- Record
- A stream for a record.
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.StreamSeq.html)- Seq
- A stream for a sequence.

# sval_ref - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sval_ref/2.20.0/sval_ref/index.html

## Expand description

A variant of [ sval::Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sval/value/trait.Value.html) for types that store references internally.

Add the `ref` feature to `sval_derive`:

```
[dependencies.sval_derive]
version = "2.20.0"
features = ["ref"]
```
and include the `#[sval(ref)]` attribute when deriving `Value`:

Fields are streamed as computed by default.
Use the `#[sval(outer_ref)]` attribute for fields with external references like `&'a str`, and the `#[sval(inner_ref)]` attribute for fields with internal references like `Data<'a>`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Ref](https://docs.rs/struct.Ref.html)
- Adapt an `sval::Value``ValueRef`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Value](https://docs.rs/trait.ValueRef.html)- Ref
- A producer of structured data that stores a reference internally.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_ref.html)- ref
- Stream a value through a stream.
- [to_ref](https://docs.rs/fn.to_ref.html)
- Wrap an `sval::Value``ValueRef`
